The default close is neither confirm nor cancel: after `GRID_AUTOSELECT_S` (3 s, timed from the button RELEASE so a held button can't burn the window) with no input the grid **selects the cursor** — timeout-cancel would punish exactly the one-handed runner the grid serves; the intended flow is hold, tap to the target, lower the wrist. The grid walks the same filtered `pages_mask` BTN3 walks (§284: data-present ∩ curated, Dashboard forced), opens on the current page or the next enabled one when its data has vanished, and the top-strip page indicator tracks the cursor while open. An on-run alert banner is deferred (not drawn) while the grid is up — under the full mask its two rows would cover the title and the first cell row mid-choice; the alert TTL outlives the ~3 s grid so it re-asserts on the landing page, and a fuel reminder additionally latches into the persistent row-1 marker, so nothing is lost. Considered and rejected: replacing the long-press page-back with the grid (two tiers, no fire-on-release change) — it regressed §286's safety path, turning Back-to-start from one decisive long-press into hold-then-aim-then-confirm. Net navigation cost: the full 32-page cycle's worst case of ~16 blind presses becomes ≤ ~7 sighted actions (tap +1 / hold +4 over a visible map), and under a typical filtered mask any page is 2-4 actions. The button task owns the state machine and the deadline (hardware and sim-buttons variants alike); the ui task only renders `state::PAGE_GRID`. Host-tested (page_grid module, button grammar, widget cursor box, two ASCII preview scenes) and sim-verified end-to-end 2026-07-21 via the new `$btn3l` / `$btn3h` monitor macros.

## 289. The watch navigation graph gets mapped, and its dead ends fixed: FIN dismisses home, the stop arm is visible, grid movement is symmetric, the home clock always shows

**Decided (2026-07-21).** Mapping the full navigation graph (docs/custom_watch/navigation.md — every surface, every button edge, measured press costs) surfaced four defects, all owner-hit in the sim the same day. (1) `Finished` was a terminal state: every button but paging was inert, so the watch held the run view until reboot. BTN1 from FIN now issues `RecordCommand::Reset` — recorder back to `Idle`, home face shows, the next run opens on the Dashboard; view-state only, since the stored run committed at stop. (2) The stop guard's arm was invisible: the first BTN2 press did nothing on screen, reading as a dead button (or worse, leaving a brushed arm silently one press from ending a multi-hour run). The face now shows a 2x `STOP? BTN2` banner for the guard's own 4 s window (`stop_arm_pending` shares `STOP_CONFIRM_WINDOW_S`, so prompt and guard can't drift), outranking alert banners but yielding to the grid, where BTN2 means cancel-and-disarm. (3) §288's grid moved forward-only (+1/+4), which made the cells just behind the cursor the most expensive on the grid (a near-full lap); BTN1 — which had no in-grid role beyond a redundant second cancel — now mirrors BTN3 backward (tap −1, hold −4, Garmin's up/down idiom), cutting the full-mask worst case from 9 to 6 actions and the average to 3.7 (the map's cost table carries the numbers). Still swallowed: no in-grid press reaches the recorder. (4) The idle face's bottom row preferred cumulative vert over the wall clock, so a baro-equipped watch showed no time of day at all; the clock (UTC — tier 1 has no timezone source) now wins whenever a fix carries it, vert keeping the row only on a GPS-less bench. Also: `pnpm watch:sim:gui:idle` boots the sim to the home face (`--no-autostart` existed; the script makes it the obvious path), since evaluating any of this from the sim's auto-started run was itself a navigation trap.

## 290. BTN4 doubles as a tap page-back on a finished run — the lap key is dead in FIN

**Decided (2026-07-22).** Owner-hit in the sim: reviewing a finished run's pages, the only leftward movement was the BTN3 long-press (§289's grammar), which reads as "there is no back button" when everything else is a tap — and a GUI-sim mouse click can't comfortably hold a threshold. In `Finished` the lap is meaningless (`command_for(Lap, Finished)` was already `None`), so the press gets the obvious meaning instead of staying dead: `watch_core::button::btn4_action` maps Recording/Paused → Lap (pinned in lockstep with `command_for` by a test) and Finished → PageBack, and both button-task variants walk `page.prev_in(mask)` on it. Recording keeps BTN4 strictly as Lap — a mid-run tap-back would trade a §81 core control for navigation sugar, so mid-run leftward stays the BTN3 long-press / grid. Idle stays inert (amended by §291: BTN4 while idle now toggles the diagnostics view). Inside §81's five-button, no-chord budget: no new gesture, just a dead press repurposed where its old meaning cannot apply.

## 291. The idle face becomes a real home face — generated 32x48 numeral clock hero, diagnostics demoted behind BTN4

**Decided (2026-07-22).** The idle face was the bench acquisition view (§289's known gap made flesh): nine identical 8x16 label-value rows, LAT/LON to five decimals on the screen a wearer sees all day. Two changes, and the panel's power story only improves. (1) A real home layout: an `HH:MM` clock hero drawn from a new 32x48 numeral face generated by `drivers/sharp_mip/scripts/gen_bignum.py` from Source Code Pro Bold — the same rasterise-a-real-font pipeline (and SIL OFL license) as `gen_font.py`, ~2.3 KiB of flash — rather than integer-scaling the 8x16 text font, whose 1-2 px strokes blow up into the ragged blocks that made the old 3x hero look home-made. Under the hero: one HR + baro-preferred ALT summary row, the GPS glance with the hero's UTC label, and the BTN3 mode read-out. The hero extrapolates the minute from the last fix's wall clock plus uptime (an Expedition-cadence fix must not freeze the clock) and is minute-resolution by design: the MIP panel charges for *changed lines*, and where the old face's seconds row redrew every fix, the hero flips once a minute — the redesign strictly reduces dirty lines. `Framebuffer::draw_bignum_band` composes whole lines and compare-writes them, so a resting clock flushes zero lines (pinned by test). (2) The bench view survives verbatim as the diagnostics face behind BTN4 while idle (`btn4_action`: Idle → ToggleDiagnostics, amending §290's "idle stays inert" — every state now gives the key exactly one meaning), snapping back to Home when a finished run is dismissed. Bring-up still gets raw LAT/LON, SPD, and the seconds clock; they just no longer masquerade as a watch face.

## 292. Typography + inverse banners + field grid — the run view adopts the designed numeral faces, banners go inverse video, the dashboard gets hairline dividers

**Decided (2026-07-22).** Three display-quality moves that finish what §291's clock hero started, none touching the recording math. (1) `gen_bignum.py` grows a 16x32 medium face and a `.` glyph alongside the 32x48 set, and the Distance / Pace glance heroes render from them via `Framebuffer::draw_bignum_hero` — glyphs before the first `.` or `:` in the big face, the rest in the medium face on a shared, table-derived baseline (big integers, smaller decimals / seconds — the Garmin idiom), replacing the pixel-scaled `draw_text_3x` blocks, which are deleted; the state tag moves to the label row so the numerals own the full band. (2) The alert / armed-stop / OFF COURSE / QNH-rezero banners are now **inverse video** (`Framebuffer::draw_banner_2x`: a solid full-width band with the centred 2x text knocked out light). The code had claimed the 1-bit panel "has no inverse video to spend" — wrong: inverse video on a plain framebuffer is just fg/bg swapped at draw time, and it is the loudest treatment a reflective panel with no backlight can give; the stale comment is corrected where it lived. (3) The run dashboard gets a Garmin-style hairline field grid — 1-px rules between its field rows plus a vertical rule splitting the NOW | GAP pair — via `Framebuffer::draw_text_row_ruled`, which composes the rules into the row's own compare-write (a separate rule pass would re-dirty the rule lines every frame) and starts them past the icon gutter so an icon blit can't re-clear them; the zero-flush-at-rest property is pinned by test. Sim-verified on the emulated panel: big-and-medium heroes on both glance pages, the `! DRINK` and `STOP? BTN2` and `OFF COURSE` bands in inverse, the ruled dashboard, and the fuel-overdue marker surviving right of the span-scoped hero.

## 293. The watch home clock tells local time — settings-frame v2 carries the phone's auto-sourced timezone offset, honestly labelled

**Decided (2026-07-22).** §291's clock hero shipped UTC-labelled because tier 1 had no timezone source; this closes that gap without growing an on-watch setting. The `SET1` frame takes its promised version bump (§284 saturated v1's flag byte): version 2 appends a second presence byte (`flags2`), whose first bit carries `tz_offset_min` — an i16 LE, minutes east of UTC. `decode` still accepts v1 frames (an old phone's push keeps working, it just carries no offset) and stays fail-closed everywhere else: an unknown `flags2` bit, a short buffer, or trailing bytes reject the whole frame, and both the full v2 and tz-only vectors are golden-pinned Rust↔Dart alongside the frozen v1 vector as a compat pin. The offset is **auto-sourced, not asked for**: the phone folds `DateTime.now().timeZoneOffset` into every settings push (injectable in tests), so the watch tells whatever time the runner's phone tells — no second clock preference to forget before a trip. On the watch the plausibility guard rides the same reject-don't-clamp discipline as the QNH field (±14 h — a clamped clock would be confidently wrong), the guarded value flows over a dedicated `state::TZ_OFFSET_MIN` watch to the ui task, and the home clock hero shifts UTC → local **with its row-7 label flipping UTC → LOCAL off the same input**, so the label can't disagree with the hero; no offset synced yet keeps the honest UTC label, and the diagnostics view deliberately stays raw receiver UTC (it is the bench view). The sim's phone-link TCP bridge became two-directional for this — `phone::settings_rx` decodes `SET1` frames off UARTE1's RX (idle-gap framed) into the same seam the BLE characteristic feeds — which is how the whole path was sim-verified live: a pushed +5:45 frame flipped the emulated panel 07:30 UTC → 13:16 LOCAL, a bad-flags2 frame rejected, and a v1 push still applied.

## 294. The watch gets a battery gauge: a probe-and-park SAADC task, a host-tested 1S LiPo curve, and an idle-face icon with a curve-knee low state

**Decided (2026-07-22).** Tier-1 had no battery read-out at all — on a device whose whole thesis is multi-day runtime, the wearer couldn't see the one number that ends the run. The new `battery` task samples the supply through the SAADC's internal VDD channel once per 60 s (state of charge moves over hours; anything faster is an unjustifiable standing wake per README § Power discipline) and publishes change-only to `state::BATTERY`. The millivolts→percent map is the host-tested `watch_core::battery`: piecewise-linear over published 1S LiPo resting-discharge anchors rather than a straight 3.3–4.2 V line, because the real curve is flat through the 3.7–3.9 V plateau and a linear map misreads a mid-run cell by ~15–20 points. The task wears the hr/baro probe-and-park posture with the park doing double duty, but NOT their `with_timeout` idiom, which the first sim run proved is an executor-wedge here: embassy-nrf's `Saadc::sample()` fires TASKS_STOP and busy-waits EVENTS_STOPPED on both its completion and its cancel-drop path, so timeout-dropping the probe future on a machine where no SAADC event ever fires (Renode's nRF52840 has no SAADC model) spun the whole executor forever — the defmt stream froze at boot. The probe instead races the first conversion against a timer WITHOUT cancelling: if the timer wins, the task parks with the probe future alive and never polled again — nothing is dropped, nothing spins — and on silicon, where the SAADC is an internal peripheral whose conversions always complete in microseconds, the probe resolves immediately and the steady loop carries no timeout at all. The second park is a plausibility band (`3200..=4350 mV`) on a rail that is not a 1S LiPo — the DK powered from USB regulates VDD to ~3.0 V, and mapping a regulator rail would render a confident 0 % lie. Parked or blanked means `None`, and every consumer shows its honest absent state (no icon, no BAT row), never a fabricated percent. Display: the idle faces carry a battery icon (body + terminal nub + proportional fill) left of the GPS signal meter, decision split per §216 — `fill_fraction` / `is_low` in `watch_core::battery`, pixels in `watch_render` — yielding the title band to the BTN3 hint and transient banners; at or below the 20 % curve knee (`LOW_PCT`, the 3.74 V anchor where the plateau ends and remaining runtime cliffs) a steady exclamation joins the body — steady, because animations are gated to the post-press window, inside which this icon doesn't draw at all. The diagnostics face adds a numeric `BAT n%` right-anchored on its HR row via an `apply_fuel_marker`-style post-pass that refuses rather than truncates a neighbour. Two accuracy caveats are recorded, not hidden: the percent is a rest-voltage estimate (a loaded cell sags below the anchors), and the default SAADC range (gain 1/6, 3.6 V full scale) rails below a fresh 4.2 V charge on a direct-VDD read — the tier-1 enclosure's cell belongs on the VDDH/5 channel + high-voltage mode, a bench follow-up noted in the README. Host-tested (curve, plausibility, low state, face row, widget geometry) and compile-verified on the default/ble/sim builds; sim-verified only that the task parks cleanly and the faces render without it — the SAADC cannot be meaningfully sampled in Renode, so the sampling path itself is bench-gated on the dev kit, the same posture as BLE.

## 295. Voice cues become a per-cue registry; race guidance speaks corrections, not verdicts; 10-10-10 is a phase-plan preset; marker targets live in marker meta

**Decided (2026-07-22, issues #607–#609).** Four connected choices. (1) Per-cue customization is ONE device-scoped settings key, `voice_cue_types` — a map of cue id → bool where an **absent id is on** — not eight separate registry keys: new cue types default audible with no migration, the pull path merges entry-by-entry so an older build's bag can't erase toggles it doesn't know, and the registry grows one row instead of one per cue forever (turn-by-turn keeps its pre-existing local pref; it predates the map). (2) Race cues speak the *correction*, never just the verdict: the pace alert says "speed up by 15 seconds per kilometre" (rounded to 5 s — sub-5 s residue isn't actionable mid-run), and the new cutoff catch-up cue derives `requiredPaceSecPerKm` inside the `live_cutoff_eta` pair — computed even when the fix is stale, because unlike the ETA it doesn't depend on recent pace — with an honest "the time limit has passed" when no pace can make it, throttled to status-changes-immediately / two-minute repeats. (3) The 10-10-10 marathon strategy ships as a preset of a general `race_phases` pair (distance-proportional phases, final-phase pace factor DERIVED so the distance-weighted mean is exactly 1.0 — hardcoding it would drift the plan off the goal time), so negative-split/even came free and future presets are data, not code. The executed strategy is stamped into `runs.metadata.pacing_strategy` (preset + distance + goal only — the plan is derivable, so it isn't stored). (4) Per-marker target times are `target_elapsed_s`/`target_clock` in the existing `route_markers.meta` jsonb (a `parseTarget` sibling of `parseCutoff`), not a new column or table: targets are per-marker facts with exactly the cutoff vocabulary's shape, every kind may carry one, and the roadbook's projected arrivals can seed them one-click (owner-only "save as marker targets"). Recording stays mobile-only (§235), so all cue *wiring* is mobile; web carries the twinned pure logic.

## 296. Route markers get viewer contributions (personal overlay); segments were already community-shared

**Decided (2026-07-23, viewer-contributed course markers).** Course markers move from owner-only to a **viewer-contribution** model: any signed-in user may add their OWN markers to a route they can see (public / club / own); UPDATE/DELETE stay own-markers-only; and a viewer's markers are a **private personal overlay** — visible only to their author, never to the route owner or other viewers. The owner's markers ("official" = `marker.user_id == route.user_id`) stay authoritative and read-only to everyone else. Enforced entirely in RLS (migration `20270428_001`): INSERT relaxes to `is_route_visible_to`, UPDATE/DELETE gate on `auth.uid() = user_id`, the base SELECT policy returns own + official via a new `private.route_owner_id` SECURITY DEFINER helper (so the official-marker check doesn't read `routes` RLS from inside a policy and return null), and `route_markers_for_viewer` returns own + owner-official (still privacy-zone-clipped for non-owners). No schema column change — `user_id` already recorded the author. 20 pgtap cases pin the boundary.

**Segments needed no backend change.** They were designed Strava-style (`20260526_001`): anyone who can read the route can create a segment, author OR route owner can delete. Only the CLIENT gated the "New segment" form to the route owner; that gate is now the signed-in viewer, with a per-row delete gated on author-or-owner (`canDeleteSegment`) so the UI never offers a delete the backend would reject. Segments stay COMMUNITY-shared (shared leaderboards), not a private overlay — the deliberate difference from markers.

**Placement by distance.** The marker editor accepts a "distance along route" (mi/km) resolved to a point on the polyline via `markerPointAtDistance` (`route_geometry.ts ↔ .dart`); the server still derives `position_m`, so the distance input is purely a client convenience over map-tap / lat-lng. `isOfficialMarker` / `markerPointAtDistance` are TS↔Dart parity twins.

## 297. OS "Open with" / share-target imports a GPX/KML as a route (device-led): octet-stream is required for WhatsApp, iOS gets document-open now and the share-sheet later

**Decided (2026-07-23).** Registered the mobile apps as an OS handler for GPX/KML files so a route received in WhatsApp (or Files / Drive / email) can be opened straight into the route library instead of forcing a save-then-import round trip. This is device-led per §24 — OS file association is a platform capability with no web equivalent — so it's a legitimate mobile-first addition. The handed-over file is delivered by `receive_sharing_intent` to `lib/shared_file_import.dart`, which reuses the existing `RouteParser` + `LocalRouteStore` import path (the routes-screen file-picker's parse dispatch was extracted into the shared `routeFromImportedFile` so the two entry points can't diverge) and, on success, opens the imported route on `RouteDetailScreen` through a global `incomingRouteImport` handoff — mirroring the `pendingStartWorkout` pattern rather than threading state through the widget tree. Every failure mode (unreadable file, unknown format, unparseable content) collapses to one "couldn't import" banner. The format is resolved by filename extension with a content root-element sniff (`<gpx`/`<kml`) fallback, because WhatsApp caches a shared `.gpx` as `application/octet-stream` and the OS copy can arrive without a usable extension.

Two deliberate trade-offs. (1) The Android `ACTION_VIEW` filter includes `application/octet-stream`: neither `.gpx` nor `.kml` is in Android's built-in MIME map, so WhatsApp hands the document over as octet-stream and Threkir would not appear in its "Open with" chooser without it — at the cost of also appearing for other unknown-binary files (guarded by validating on parse and falling to the failure banner). The specific `application/gpx+xml` / `…kml+xml` types plus a file-scheme extension `pathPattern` cover the sources that type the file (Files, Drive). `ACTION_SEND` mirrors the same MIME set for the "Share → Threkir" sheet. (2) iOS ships document "Open with" now (`CFBundleDocumentTypes` + imported UTIs `com.topografix.gpx` / `com.google.earth.kml`, no Share Extension needed); the iOS *system share sheet* additionally requires a Share Extension target (new Xcode target + App Group + on-device testing) and is deferred as a follow-up. The delivery logic is unit-tested (`shared_file_import_test.dart` — format detection, content-sniff, success + every failure path), but the OS-integration behaviour itself needs on-device end-to-end verification (mobile has no e2e harness by design).

## 298. Route sharing gets a mobile "Share link", starting a public route you don't own is a first-class action, and both ride a global start-run handoff

**Decided (2026-07-23).** Three connected choices around "share a route to a follower, and let them run it".

(1) **Mobile gains a one-tap "Share link"** on route-detail (`route_detail_screen`) — the intuitive send-to-someone path web already had (`routes/[id]/+page.svelte`'s `handleShare`), which mobile lacked (it only exported GPX/KML/image files). It flips a still-private route public (owner only, `routeDetailMadePublicForLink` banner) and hands the `/share/route/{id}` URL (`routeShareUrl`, host from `WEB_BASE_URL`) to the OS share sheet, so the user picks WhatsApp / a DM / any app → the follower. The menu item is gated to `_isPublic || _isOwner` so a non-owner can never share a dead (non-public) link.

(2) **Starting a public route you don't own is now first-class.** `public_route_screen` (the read-only `/share/route/[id]` mirror a follower lands on, and the club/heatmap route viewer) gained a **Start run** FAB + a **Save to my routes** (bookmark) action — previously it was view-only, so a shared route couldn't actually be run. Start carries the CLIPPED display waypoints, never the owner's full trace (`publicRouteStartTarget`, privacy-relevant, unit-tested). Recording is a device capability (§235), so this is mobile-only with no web parity to close; the web equivalent (save a public route to your library) already exists via RouteExplorer.

(3) **A global `pendingStartRunWithRoute` notifier replaces the fragile pop-based start.** The route-detail "Start run" FAB used to `Navigator.pop(context, route)` and rely on whoever pushed the screen to catch the returned route and start the run — so Start silently did nothing from any pusher that didn't (the shared-file import landing from §297, a deep push, the public-route screen). It now sets a global notifier (sibling of `pendingStartWorkout`); HomeScreen listens, preselects the route, jumps to the recorder, and `popUntil(isFirst)` dismisses the pushed screen. The existing `routes_screen` / `explore_routes` flows are unchanged and un-broken — their `if (picked != null) onStartRun(...)` guards simply no-op now that the FAB returns nothing, and the notifier does the work. Cleaning up the now-vestigial `onStartRun` callback plumbing is a follow-up, not this change.

**"Send to a follower" in-app (targeted, not a link) is specced web-first, not built here.** A DM rail already exists (`direct_messages` + web `/messages`), so v1 is a route action that opens the DM composer prefilled with the share link (`sendDm(followerId, url)`) — no schema change; v2 adds a typed route attachment so it renders as a card. Web-canonical per §24. Spec: [route_direct_share.md](../features/route_direct_share.md).

**Amendment (2026-07-23) — confirm before the public flip.** The owner-facing half of (1) now asks first: on both web (`ConfirmDialog`, `data-testid="share-confirm-dialog"`) and mobile (`AlertDialog`), tapping Share on a *still-private* route opens a confirm ("Make this route public?") before `setRoutePublic`, because that flip exposes the route (and its start point) to anyone with the link and surfaces it in Explore — a privacy-relevant, one-way-for-now step, so it should be a deliberate yes rather than a side effect of tapping Share. An **already-public** route still shares in one tap (nothing changes), and the post-flip `…MadePublicForLink` disclosure banner stays as the "here's what happened" confirmation. Pinned by a web e2e in `detail.spec.ts` (cancel keeps it private + reveals no link; confirm flips public + reveals the link) and a mobile widget test in `route_detail_screen_test.dart`.

---

## 299. A damaged run-sync sidecar falls back to the index, and never presumes a run synced — the opposite default to the route store

**Decided (2026-07-25).** `LocalRunStore`'s `synced_ids.json` sidecar is the authoritative record of which runs have reached the server; `markSynced` writes it and deliberately does not rewrite the per-run file or the index. When that sidecar is unreadable the store now resolves sync state in a fixed authority order — sidecar, then `index.json`'s cached `synced` flag (rewritten from the authoritative set on every mutation, so it can only lag toward "unsynced"), then the legacy per-run flag, which is consulted **only** when no sidecar was ever written (a genuine pre-sidecar install, where it is the real record).

This is intentionally *not* the fail-closed presumed-synced default `LocalRouteStore` adopted for the same corruption. The two failure directions are not symmetric across the two stores. For routes, re-pushing the library also re-owns it (`tagRoutesOwner` stamps the current user), so a wrong push is a cross-account transfer and skipping a push is merely wasteful. For runs the reverse holds: an upload we repeat costs bandwidth and upserts by id, while a run wrongly presumed synced never drains again — and a recorded run is often the only copy of something that happened. So runs re-upload rather than risk silence.

Fixing the tri-state also exposed the ordering bug underneath it: the slow-path repair called `_persistSyncedIds()` *before* `_summaries` was rebuilt, and that method prunes the set against `_summaries`. Every id recovered on the full-walk path was therefore dropped and an empty sidecar durably written — so the legacy migration path had never worked, and any drifted index re-uploaded the entire local history. The repair write now runs after `_summaries` exists. Pinned across five corruption shapes plus the no-index and legacy-migration paths.

---

## 300. The hydration card's exercise add-on stops scaling at four hours

**Decided (2026-07-25).** `hydrationTargetMl` adds 8 ml of water per logged exercise minute on top of the ~35 ml/kg baseline. That term was unbounded, and both callers feed it the day's *total* active minutes — so a logged 12 h ultra asked for ~8.2 L (33 water pips) and a 24 h effort ~14 L. The add-on now stops at `MAX_EXERCISE_MINUTES` / `maxExerciseMinutes` = 240, capping it at 1.92 L.

A ceiling is the conservative direction, which is why it ships rather than waiting: telling a runner who just finished a hundred-miler to drink 14 L is an exercise-associated-hyponatremia risk stated as a goal, and the unbounded version had no evidence behind it above an hour — it is a daily-baseline heuristic being extrapolated four to twenty-four times past its range. Long-effort fluid is already modelled properly elsewhere: `fuel_plan` allocates per leg against aid stations with carbs alongside, which is the surface that should answer "how much do I drink during a 12 h race".

**The specific number is a product call the owner can tune, not a clinical recommendation** — four hours is chosen as the point past which a daily water goal stops being the right instrument, not as a physiological limit. Sweat rates vary roughly 0.5–2.0 L/h by athlete and conditions, so a per-athlete sweat-rate input (or a hand-off to the fuel plan once a long effort is logged) is the better long-term answer; this ceiling is the safe floor under it. Twin-pinned on both platforms (11 tests each).

---

## 301. A watch-ingest payload that cannot be parsed is quarantined and swept, not retried forever or deleted on sight

**Decided (2026-07-25).** `WatchIngestQueue.drain` treated every failure the same: log it, leave the file, move on. That conflates two opposite classes. An upload failure is transient and must keep retrying — that is the queue's entire purpose. A read/decode failure is permanent: the bytes will not improve, so the entry was re-read on every sign-in forever and `pendingCount` reported a phantom queued run the user could never clear. `enqueue` also used a bare `writeAsString` while every sibling store used `writeStringAtomic`, so a process death mid-write manufactured exactly those unparseable files; it is now atomic.

The two classes are now split at the seam: parse (read → decode → envelope detection → `runFromWatchPayload`) versus upload (`api.saveRun`). A parse failure renames the file to `<uuid>.json.rejected`, which drops it out of the `.json` glob every listing here uses — so it stops being retried and stops counting as pending — and a sweep at `init` deletes rejected entries past 30 days.

Renaming rather than deleting is the deliberate middle: deleting on sight would let a decoder bug silently destroy a real recorded run, while keeping it forever is residue that carries GPS. The 30-day sweep mirrors the bounded-retention rule `LocalCrossingsStore` adopted, and `rejectedCount` is test-visible so the retry-forever regression stays pinned.

**Amended 2026-07-25 (same day).** Three gaps in the same split. (1) A payload with **no `id`** landed on the wrong side of it: `runFromWatchPayload` substituted `''`, so decoding "succeeded" and the permanent failure surfaced from `api.saveRun`, where every error is classified transient — Postgres rejects `''` as a uuid on every attempt, so the entry retried on every sign-in forever. A missing or blank id is now a `FormatException`, which routes it to the quarantine the parse side already has. Neither shipped sender omits `id` (Wear's `WatchRunMetadata`, watchOS's `syncRun`), so no live sender changes behaviour; two tests that pinned the `''` fallback pinned a path that could never have worked. (2) `setLastKnownOwner` was still a bare `writeAsString` while `enqueue` was atomic — and `init` reads an empty file as "no owner", so a kill mid-write dropped the stamp and let the next account adopt the previous user's run. It now uses `writeStringAtomic`, and `watch_ingest_queue.dart` is in the `noBareWriteStores` architecture guard. (3) Those atomic writes leave `.tmp` orphans; the queue sweeps them at `init` (see § 313).

---

## 302. A drained row is marked synced by identity, not by id — and a store drains one at a time

**Decided (2026-07-25).** `OfflineSyncStore.syncWithServer` snapshots the rows, awaits a network push per row, then called `markSynced(id)`, which flipped *whatever was resident at that later moment* to `synced`. An edit made during the push was therefore recorded as sent when it had not been: `replaceFromServer`'s newer-wins then preserves the local copy, so the client and the server diverge permanently and neither side can see it. The delete-during-push variant was worse — the fresh tombstone was flipped to `synced`, so the server row survived with no local record that it should be gone.

`markSynced` now takes the pushed entry and only marks it when it is still `identical` to the resident row; the `pendingDelete` branch applies the same test before `dropRow`. Identity is the exact test here because entries are immutable value objects and every mutation installs a new instance — there is no in-place edit to miss. A false negative (a same-content instance swapped in by an unrelated path) costs one extra drain, which is the harmless direction. A `lastModifiedAt` comparison was the alternative and is strictly weaker: two mutations inside one clock tick would compare equal.

`syncWithServer` also gained a re-entrancy guard, mirroring `SyncService._syncing`. `session_detail_screen` fires it unawaited and several screens drain on both a manual refresh and a connectivity return, so two concurrent drains over one store were reachable — they would push the same row twice and race each other's state writes. A second concurrent call returns 0 rather than queueing, matching the count-for-a-banner contract callers already have. All eight subclasses inherit both changes.

---

## 303. The run store's sidecars merge under a cross-process lock, because two isolates own the same directory

> **Amended 2026-07-25 (same day).** As first written this entry described the change as covering `LocalRunStore` **and** `LocalRouteStore`. Only the run store was actually changed — the merge and `_withSidecarLock` never reached `local_route_store.dart`, and `followups.md` repeated the same wrong claim. The route store's three sidecars have now been brought over; the rules they use are below, after the run-store rules, because they resolve a shared id in the OPPOSITE direction.

**Decided (2026-07-25).** `background_sync.dart` constructs its own `LocalRunStore` + `LocalRouteStore` in the WorkManager isolate, over the same on-disk directory the foreground stores use. Both run sidecars — `synced_ids.json` and `pending_remote_deletes.json` — were whole-file writes from one process's in-memory snapshot, so each write silently discarded whatever the other had done since that snapshot was taken. `pending_remote_deletes` was the dangerous one: the old code *deleted the file* when its map was empty, so a background drain that loaded before the foreground queued a remote delete wiped that delete outright and the run stayed on the server with nothing left to retry it. The `synced_ids` clobber "only" cost a full-track re-upload.

Both writes are now read-merge-write inside an exclusive advisory lock (`<sidecar>.lock`, `FileLock.blockingExclusive`, best-effort — a failed lock still performs the merged write, which beats no write). Merging alone closes the whole-file discard; the lock closes the remaining interleave where two merges race.

The merge rules differ because the two sidecars fail in opposite directions:

- **`synced_ids`** — ids this process knows about are decided by its own `_syncedIds`, so a run it deliberately holds unsynced can't be resurrected from a stale file. An unknown id is kept only if its run FILE still exists, which is the process-independent version of the "no local row ⇒ prune the ghost" rule the old code approximated with `_summaries` (this process's view only).
- **`pending_remote_deletes`** — additions always win, and removals are carried by an explicit `_clearedRemoteDeletes` ledger rather than inferred from absence, because absence cannot distinguish "I cleared this" from "they queued this while I was running". The ledger resets after each successful write, at which point disk already reflects our removals. The asymmetry is deliberate: re-deleting an already-deleted row is a no-op, losing a queued delete is unrecoverable.

`LocalRouteStore`'s three sidecars — `synced_route_ids.json`, `route_owner_tags.json`, `offline_pinned_route_ids.json` — now take the same lock, but all three resolve a **shared** id the `pending_remote_deletes` way (additions win, removals travel by ledger) rather than the `synced_ids` way (this process decides every id it knows). That is not inconsistency, it is § 299's asymmetry applied to the other store. `drainUnsyncedRoutes` calls `markManyRoutesSynced` **and** `tagRoutesOwner` from the background isolate for routes the foreground also holds, so the "this process decides" rule would let a foreground `save()` from a pre-drain snapshot revert both — dropping the route back to unsynced (a re-push, which for routes also re-owns) and back to untagged (visible to, and drainable by, every account on a shared device). For runs the losing direction is a run that never drains; for routes it is another user's route copied into this account's cloud, which is not recoverable. So routes keep the addition.

Concretely: `_syncedIdsCleared` / `_offlinePinnedCleared` carry set removals and `_ownerTagsTouched` carries the map's set-and-drop, each cleared after a successful write. `synced_route_ids` additionally prunes an id for a route this process no longer holds whose file is gone (the growth bound `_persistSyncedIds` has); the offline pins deliberately do not, because pinning an id before its route lands is a supported forward-looking intent.

**Amended 2026-08-03.** `LocalRouteStore` grew a fourth sidecar, `pending_remote_route_deletes.json` (the delete-retry queue), after this decision landed — and it shipped with the old unlocked whole-map overwrite, carrying the same bug this entry fixed for the other three. It now takes `_withSidecarLock` too, merging the `pending_remote_deletes` way (additions win, removals via a `_clearedRemoteDeletes` ledger) — the same rule `LocalRunStore`'s equivalent sidecar already uses, since losing a queued route delete is exactly as unrecoverable as losing a queued run delete.

---

## 304. Gym adherence matches planned to actual by expanded-step ordinal, not by the per-block set index

**Decided (2026-07-25).** `computeRoutineAdherence` keyed its planned↔actual match on `(exerciseKey, setIndex)`. `setIndex` is the position of a set *within its exercise block* and restarts in each block, so a routine that programs the same exercise twice — the heavy-top-set-then-back-off pattern, which is ordinary strength programming — minted identical keys for two different planned sets. Both collapsed onto one logged set: a perfectly executed session graded 50% / `partial`, the deltas were lifted off the wrong set, and the heavy top set was neither graded nor surfaced as `extra`. The persisted `gym_step_results` row carried the other block's targets for the same reason. Both twins had it, and all 24 cases in each suite happened to use distinct keys.

The match identity is now `stepIndex`: the ref's ordinal position in the expanded step list, stamped by the runner that builds the list. `setIndex` stays on the ref for display. Both runners pass the ordinal, and the persisted row now carries `step_index` — which `gym_programming.md` § P3 had specced from the start; only the implementation omitted it.

Two alternatives were rejected. **Consume-in-order matching** (each planned ref takes the first unclaimed actual with its key) needs no new field, but it mis-pairs the moment a set is skipped — and a skipped set is precisely what adherence exists to measure. **Renumbering `setIndex` to be routine-global** would fix the key but overload a field whose per-block meaning the editor, the DB rows, and the display all depend on.

Test factories on both sides default `stepIndex` to `setIndex`, which is exactly true for the single-block routines every pre-existing case uses — so the 24 existing cases are unchanged and the new two-block case passes the ordinal explicitly.

---

## 305. Elevation gain is one contract: the raw track, a 3 m noise gate, and a dropout that carries rather than breaks

**Decided (2026-07-25).** `computeElevationGain` existed three times with three behaviours, and each suite pinned its own.

- **Null handling diverged across the twin.** Dart carried the last valid reading across an altitude dropout (its doc comment declared this intentional); TS required both members of a pair to be non-null, so any dropout broke the chain. For `ele = [100, null, null, 130, 120, 125]` Dart returned 35 and TS returned 5 — and `route_simplify.test.ts` asserted the TS value with a comment enshrining it, so both suites passed side by side forever while both files' doc comments claimed they were kept in sync.
- **The input diverged too.** Web's `summarizeRouteFromTrack` measured gain over the **2-D-simplified** polyline. RDP ignores elevation, so a dead-straight road over a summit collapses to its endpoints and 50 m of real climb saved as 0. Mobile measured over the **raw** track with no hysteresis, so a ±5 m sawtooth at 1 Hz wrote thousands of metres of phantom vert.
- **A third inline copy** lived in `run_detail_screen`, with the adjacent-pair null rule Dart's own helper had already rejected.

One contract now, on both platforms: **gain is taken over the raw track**, a missing sample is a dropout that carries the last reading rather than a plateau that breaks the chain, and a change only counts once it clears a 3 m band in either direction (`ELEVATION_GAIN_MIN_DELTA_M` / `kElevationGainMinDeltaM`). The gate is a hysteresis reference, not a per-sample filter, so a long shallow climb is still counted in full while sample-to-sample jitter contributes nothing; the cost is that up to 3 m of a climb's final partial step is unbooked, which the tests pin explicitly rather than hide behind a tolerance.

`computeElevationLoss` moved into the same module with the same gate. It is mobile-only, but it had to move: run-detail shows loss directly beside gain, and grading one through the noise band while summing the other raw would make a flat road report 0 m of climb next to hundreds of metres of descent — a fix that reads as a bug.

`route_simplify` is now a declared parity pair in `CLAUDE.md` and in the `shared-library-syncer` agent, which is what the two doc comments had been asserting without enforcement. The pair's scope is `simplifyTrack` + `computeElevationGain` + the constant; `summarizeRouteFromTrack` stays web-only and `computeElevationLoss` mobile-only.

**Amended (2026-07-25).** There was a fourth copy: the live counter in `run_screen`'s `_onSnapshot`, which summed every positive delta between adjacent waypoints with no gate and no dropout carry. It read ~1,200 m on a flat 10K next to run-detail's ~38 m for the same track, minutes apart. It survived the unification because it is the one caller that cannot pass a finished track — it sees the track grow per GPS tick and re-scanning the whole thing each tick is O(n²) over an ultra. The fix is `ElevationGainAccumulator` in the same module: the gate and the dropout carry as streaming state, with `computeElevationGain` now being that accumulator run to completion, so there is exactly one implementation and the live figure cannot drift from the saved one. The accumulator is Dart-only and outside the parity pair's scope — web has no incremental consumer — for the same reason `computeElevationLoss` is.

---

## 306. Liveness is the age of the last accepted fix, not the presence of a position on the snapshot

**Decided (2026-07-25).** `RunRecorder`'s 1-second timer re-emits the last `_currentWaypoint` on every tick, and that field is cleared only by `prepare()`. This is deliberate — the blue dot and the follow-cam must survive a signal gap — but the run screen read "the snapshot carries a position" as "the sensor is alive", so `_lastSnapshotAt` was refreshed every second of a total GPS blackout. A runner entering a long tunnel got no red banner, no amber banner, a flat-lining distance, a cut-off ETA projected off a dead fix (exactly what `live_cutoff_eta`'s `stale` flag exists to prevent), and a spectator page that showed them as fresh and stationary because `LiveBroadcaster` kept pinging the frozen coordinate every 5 s.

The snapshot now carries `positionFixedAt` — the wall clock at the moment the fix was accepted — and one derived `positionFresh` flag gates the banner and both spectator ping paths. Three consequences worth stating:

- **Wall clock, not the GPS-reported timestamp.** `Waypoint.timestamp` is `pos.timestamp` on purpose (dt between two fixes must be the real interval even when fixes are processed in a batched tight loop), but freshness asks a different question — "how long since we last heard from the sensor" — and a device whose GPS clock is skewed would answer it with a permanent banner or a permanently fresh one. Acceptance time is measured against the same clock the threshold is.
- **Pings stop rather than repeat.** The spectator sees the last ping age into `live_freshness`'s "updated N min ago" stale bucket. That is the honest render, and it is what the SAR / crew personas need; a heartbeat carrying a coordinate we no longer believe is worse than silence.
- **A manual pause ages the fix out too**, because the recorder drops every fix while paused. The GPS-lost banner is therefore suppressed while paused (the sensor isn't lost, we're ignoring it), but the ping gate is not: a 20-minute aid-station stop reads as stale to spectators. One rule, no special case — we would rather a spectator see "updated 12 min ago" than a live dot for a position nobody is confirming.

`RunSnapshot.positionTrusted` ships in the same change and answers the sibling question. The recorder already refused to let a distance-rejected fix advance its monotonic route floor, but the bit was internal, so the screen's three route-position consumers re-derived `distanceAlongRoute` from the raw fix. One multipath teleport 4 km up the course announced the next three course markers at once and latched them in `_announcedTargetMarkers`, which is never un-latched — the runner reached those aid stations hours later in silence. The screen now keeps `_routePosition` (the last accepted fix) and routes turn cues, marker cues and the cut-off ETA through it. The cost is that route progress is only evaluated on accepted fixes, so a slow walk through an aid station evaluates crossings a couple of seconds later than before; the alternative is trusting a fix the distance chain has already judged corrupt.

## 307. A turn cue announces the distance the runner is actually at, and only the tightest band speaks

**Decided (2026-07-25).** `TurnCueAnnouncer` walked `[300, 100, 0]` and fired the first band the runner was inside, and the run screen spoke that band's number. For a route whose first turn is 120 m from the start — a corner at the end of the runner's street, the common case — the first fix fired the 300 band, the next second fired the 100 band, and a second later "turn now": three announcements in three seconds, two of them stating a distance that was false by a factor of two or three. The same burst fired whenever an along-route value jumped a band's width after a GPS gap.

Two changes, both at the root. `TurnAnnouncement` now carries `aheadM`, the runner's real distance ahead at the moment the cue was decided, and that is what is spoken; `thresholdM` is demoted to what it always was — a slot identifier for the once-per-band bookkeeping. And `announcementFor` picks the **tightest** unfired band the runner is inside, retiring the looser applicable ones silently, so a turn first seen at 120 m produces one honest "in 0.12 km" and then "now".

We chose this over the narrower "only fire a band the runner has CROSSED into" rule. Crossing detection also stops the burst, but it says nothing at all about a turn first observed inside a band — a route that starts at a corner would be announced by neither the far bands nor the "now" band, because there is no crossing to detect — and it still fires the 300 band with the 300 label after a gap that lands the runner 50 m out. Tightest-band-plus-real-distance is strictly more honest at every input and needs no per-cue previous-distance state.

---

## 308. A local run mutation is durably unsynced, and the run it touched is resident

**Decided (2026-07-25).** `LocalRunStore.update()` flipped a run to unsynced in memory and wrote `index.json` saying so — but never wrote `synced_ids.json`, which § 299 makes the **authoritative** cold-load record that overrides the index's flag. Edit a run offline, get killed before reconnecting, and the next launch re-marked it synced from the stale sidecar: the edit was local-only and permanently undrainable, and `saveFromRemote`'s newer-wins then kept the local copy, so neither side ever converged. `save()` had the same hole in the re-save case (it stamps the summary unsynced but left the id in `_syncedIds`), which is how an offline backup restore over an existing library produced a run that read as synced and never re-pushed.

Both now persist the sidecar. `update()` always does; `save()` only when the id was actually in the set, so the terminal run save — the hot path, already dominated by a full-track encode — stays one write for a brand-new id.

The second half is residency. `unsyncedRuns` reads `_runs` (the resident window), not `_summaries`, because the drain needs the GPS track. `update()` only replaced an existing entry, so editing a run outside the window never made it resident and the edit was invisible to the drain **even in the same session**. It now inserts and re-sorts, which is exactly the documented `window ∪ unsynced` invariant (§ 135) rather than an exception to it.

Downstream of making the un-sync durable, run-detail's edit path had to settle it: it pushes the edited columns with `api.updateRunFields`, which covers every field that dialog can change, so on a 2xx it now calls `markSynced`. Without that the next `SyncService` cycle runs `saveRunsBatch` and re-gzips + re-uploads the whole track — megabytes of cellular for a title edit on an ultra. A failed push leaves the run queued, which is the correct fallback.

---

## 309. `index.json` is merged per-id under the sidecar lock, because the cold-load gate only compares the id set

**Decided (2026-07-25).** § 303 gave the two sidecars a merge and a lock. `index.json` — written by the same two isolates over the same directory — got neither, and it is the one where a clobber does not self-heal. The cold-load fast path validates the index by **membership only** (`index.length == fileById.length && every id present`), so id-set drift forces a rebuild but per-id CONTENT drift passes the gate, is loaded verbatim, and is then re-persisted from memory on every subsequent write. A background isolate that cold-loaded before a foreground edit and later wrote the index for its own reasons (a drained remote delete) durably restored the pre-edit distance for every all-history consumer — yearly mileage, fitness, recap, the runs list — while run-detail, which reads the file, showed the corrected one. The stale `last_modified_at` also fed `saveFromRemote`'s newer-wins, so a delta fetch could then judge the server's older row newer.

`_persistIndex` now reads the on-disk index inside `_withSidecarLock(index.json)` and resolves each id by `_lastModifiedOf` — the same modification clock `saveFromRemote` already uses — with ties going to this process, which just wrote the file. Liveness is pruned by `File('<id>.json').existsSync()`, not against `_summaries`: `_summaries` is only this process's view, and pruning against it would delete the other isolate's rows. Cost is one extra index decode per mutation; if that ever shows up on a very large library, the fix is to skip the read when the file's mtime is unchanged since our last write, not to drop the merge.

---

## 310. A scoped server fetch may only prune its own scope

**Decided (2026-07-25).** `LocalCrossingsStore.replaceFromServer` preserved pending rows and deleted every other row not in the payload — a full-replace contract. Its only caller fetches crossings for ONE `(event_id, instance_start)` pair. So a volunteer who stamped 60 runners at Aid 3 of event E1 and then opened the check-in screen for E2 lost all 60 from memory **and from disk**, and offline — on a mountain with no signal, which is the entire reason this store exists — they never came back.

The method now takes the fetch's scope and preserves any synced row outside it, mirroring the `windowStart` / `fetchLimit` guard `LocalGymStore` and `LocalFoodStore` already carry. Both null is still a full replace, correct only when the caller genuinely fetched the complete set. Deriving the scope from the returned rows was rejected: an event with zero crossings returns an empty list and would look like "prune everything".

The `kSyncedRetention` sweep runs inside this same rebuild, so the preserved-out-of-scope rows are aged against it too — otherwise the 90-day Art 9 mirror would silently stop expiring every event except the one currently on screen.

---

## 311. The backup archives the phone, not the cloud

**Decided (2026-07-25).** `createBackup` sourced `runs.json` from `api.fetchRunRowsRaw()` and the tracks from Storage, so a run that had not drained — the drain in backoff, a failed track upload, a long offline stretch — was simply absent. It exists only in `<appDocs>/runs/<id>.json`. Nothing in the archive or the UI said so: the runner finishes a hundred-miler, takes a backup because they are about to change phones, reads a plausible `manifest.counts.runs`, wipes, restores, and the race is gone.

`createBackup` now takes the `LocalRunStore` and appends every unsynced run the server doesn't already have, gzipping its in-memory track into the same `tracks/<id>.json.gz` entry the restore path already reads and counting it in the manifest. It also **skips the server-first path entirely** while anything is local-only: the Go service builds the archive from cloud rows and cannot see this device, so taking it would produce exactly the archive this fixes.

The row shaping mirrors `ApiClient.saveRun` — built through the generated `RunRow` so column names can't drift, `user_id` and `track_url` stripped (restore stamps the new owner and re-homes the blob), and the promoted `activity_type` / `is_dnf` / `fastest_*_s` keys lifted out of the metadata bag, since the column is the only stored copy and a bag left carrying them would shadow a later edit after restore. That lift is currently duplicated from `api_client`'s private helper; the durable fix is to extract one shaper into `core_models` and point `saveRun` at it too, which is tracked in followups rather than done here because it reaches outside this change's blast radius.

The offline restore also became genuinely additive, which `restore`'s own docstring already promised and the gym / food restore already honoured. It skipped nothing: `save(run)` overwrote a same-id local run, and a track download that failed during `createBackup` is only logged — so restoring that archive replaced a full on-device GPS trace with an empty one. It now skips an id already present locally (unless `generateNewIds`, which imports everything alongside). `LocalRunStore.hasRun` is the test, not `contains`, because `contains` only sees the resident window.

`iterateAllRuns` was deleted in the same change. Its docstring claimed it backed the backup export "which must include the complete history — including unsynced runs whose track lives only in the local file"; it had no production caller, so the guarantee it stated had never been implemented anywhere.

---

## 312. `clearInProgress` drains the in-flight append before deleting

**Decided (2026-07-25).** `saveInProgress`'s guard made two *saves* mutually exclusive but said nothing about a save racing a *clear*. The periodic driver is fire-and-forget, so a tick already inside its `compute()` hop when the user taps Stop landed its append after `clearInProgress()` deleted the file — and `FileMode.writeOnlyAppend` **recreates** it. The next launch then reconstructed a `Run` with the finished run's full header and a handful of waypoints, `evaluateInProgressPartial` called it resumable, and both Resume and Finish end in `runStore.save()` under the same id, overwriting the completed run's file with the ~10-point partial.

Reported as suspected-timing; it reproduced on 32 of 60 iterations of a save-then-clear race in `local_run_store_test.dart`, so it is a live defect, not a theoretical window. The `bool _savingInProgress` is now a `Future<void>? _inFlightSave` that `clearInProgress` awaits before deleting. The await swallows a save failure deliberately — the save reports to its own caller, and a failed append is precisely the case where the delete still has to happen. `clearInProgress` becomes blocking for one isolate hop; none of its callers (`_stop`, the discard branch, `main.dart`'s recovery) is latency-critical.

---

## 313. Atomic-write orphans are swept at cold load by one shared helper

**Decided (2026-07-25).** `writeStringAtomic` leaves `<file>.<n>.tmp` behind when the process dies between flush and rename. `OfflineSyncStore` grew a sweep for these; `LocalRunStore`, `LocalRouteStore` and `WatchIngestQueue` did not, and every listing in those three filters on `.json` — so an orphan holding a full GPS track, a route's full waypoint list, or a queued watch run was invisible, never pruned, and (unlike the per-row stores, which are cleared outright on sign-out) survived an account change.

The sweep now lives in `core_models/atomic_io.dart`, next to the writer that creates the orphans, and all four cold-load paths call it. The one-hour age gate is load-bearing and must not be lowered: it is what keeps the sweep from deleting the temp file of a genuinely concurrent writer, since the background-sync isolate holds its own store instances over the same directories. For the same reason the sweep belongs at cold load, never in a write path. `atomic_io.dart` is a pure Dart package with no logger, so failures go out through an `onError` callback the Flutter callers wire to `debugPrint`.

---

## 314. The custom-watch verification ladder becomes a four-rung contract, and tier-1 bench verification gets a checklist — neither changes § 82's DoD

**Decided (2026-07-25).** Two related gaps in the custom_watch research effort, closed together in [`docs/custom_watch/quality_standards.md`](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md).

**(a) The verification vocabulary is now defined.** The docs and `apps/custom_watch/README.md` have used an informal four-rung ladder — *host-tested* → *build-verified* → *sim-verified* → *bench-verified* — since the Renode sim landed, without ever defining it anywhere; the string "bench-verified" did not appear in the workspace README at all, despite being the rung 13 of the 43 [`roadmap.md`](../custom_watch/roadmap.md) parity-backlog items are explicitly waiting on. Each rung now states what evidence earns it, what it does **not** prove, and what may be claimed in docs at it, including the honesty limits that were previously scattered across per-batch notes: the Renode sim cannot run the proprietary S140 SoftDevice, so **BLE can never be sim-verified** and jumps build → bench directly ([§ 210](#210-tier-1-ble-s140-softdevice-is-a-compile-verified-feature-gated-build--mutually-exclusive-with-the-sim-off-by-default)); the sim models no current at all, so every power figure in the workspace is a derivation; the sensor models are pinned to what the drivers *believe* about the parts, not to silicon, so they verify the path and not the register semantics; and the DK's ~30 mA idle from its onboard J-Link + LEDs makes whole-device power readings useless as a baseline ([§ 83](#83-tier-1-power-measurement-uses-nordic-power-profiler-kit-ii-applied-per-subsystem)). Three rules ride along: a rung is **not inherited** (editing a bench-verified module drops it to whatever the new evidence supports), a rung claim must name its evidence, and a lower rung may never stand in for a higher one in a doc line.

**(b) Tier-1 bench verification is now a checklist, not a vibe.** Before this, tier 1 had a completion bar (§ 82 — one outdoor run syncing end-to-end) and *no* falsifiable hardware-side standard: no fix-reliability threshold, no legibility check, no per-subsystem current criterion, no storage-boundary check. Tier 2 has real targets (≥ 24 hr GPS battery, 100 % outdoor fix reliability); tier 1 had none, so "did bring-up work?" would have been decided by feel the day the parts arrive. The new doc carries a per-bring-up-step checklist (steps 0 and 3–7 plus the five § 83 PPK2 rigs) where every item is a yes/no or a number. The concrete criteria are **derived from figures already in the docs**, not invented — the ≤ 60 s cold TTFF, the 1 Hz fix rate, the ~25 Hz HR sampling, the ≥ 8 h continuous-GPS soak and the printed-chassis deliverable all come from [`prototyping.md`](../custom_watch/prototyping.md)'s tier-1 "what working means"; the sync-row match, wrist-worn run and pace-on-panel items come from § 82 itself; the 253-point cap, 4 × 4 KiB slots, 256-point course cap, 40 m/20 m off-course latch, 0.5 m/s auto-pause and the press-timing tiers come from the firmware's own constants. Where no existing doc justified a number it is marked **(open value)** to be set from the first real measurement rather than invented — warm-start TTFF, acceptable dropout rate, HR accuracy tolerance, off-axis legibility, AGC convergence, and any tier-1 sleep-current target.

**What this deliberately does not do.** **§ 82's Definition of Done is unchanged and remains the only tier-1 completion bar.** The checklist governs how bench verification is *conducted and claimed*, not whether tier 1 is done: one qualifying outdoor run completes tier 1 even with checklist items open, and an open or failed item is a recorded finding and a tier-2 input, not an un-completion. Nor does it import tier-2's targets, add kill criteria (§ 82 declined to set them and that holds), or expand scope past § 71's owner-personal boundary — the doc carries an explicit "what tier 1 does not have to hit" section naming the ≥ 24 hr battery, 100 % fix reliability, dual-band GNSS, in-case RF, IPX7, multi-run and OTA/maps/ANT+ exclusions so the checklist cannot be read as scope creep. A third section enumerates the figures the checklist exists to settle — the ~110/180/220 h GNSS-mode battery projections (derivations that already *assume* a receiver power-down never run on a receiver), the HR duty-cycle saving deliberately excluded from them, the battery-percent resting-discharge curve, the checkpoint flash-wear estimate, the bench-prototype capacity limits (253-point run cap, 256-point course cap, 64-lap budget), the sensor-tuning constants flagged for on-device calibration, and the one structural assumption that is not a number at all: that the MAX86177 retains its register file across `shutdown()`, which the firmware's wake path depends on and no silicon has confirmed.

Don't re-litigate by:

- **Treating a red checklist item as blocking tier-1 completion.** It isn't. § 82 is the gate; this is the instrumentation.
- **Promoting a checklist item into the DoD** because it looks important. That is the goal-post drift § 82 was written to prevent — the same reason it pinned the bar at one run.
- **Filling in an (open value) with a plausible-looking figure** rather than a measurement. An invented threshold is worse than an admitted gap: it reads as measured to the next person.
- **Claiming a rung the evidence doesn't support** — in particular using "sim-verified" to tick a parity-backlog item, or reading "compile-verified" BLE as anything other than "the dependency stack links".

Pinning: [`docs/custom_watch/quality_standards.md`](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md) holds the rung definitions + the checklist; [`roadmap.md`](../custom_watch/roadmap.md) links it from the per-step bring-up, Definition-of-Done, power-instrumentation and parity-backlog sections; [`tier1_log.md`](../custom_watch/tier1_log.md) is where bench evidence lands. `apps/custom_watch/README.md` is the per-step status surface and should point at this doc for what its rung words mean.

## 315. custom_watch CI gates all three firmware feature sets, not just the default build

**Decided (2026-07-25).** The `build-firmware` job built and clippy-gated only the **default** feature set, so two of the three real builds were defended by nothing but a per-batch manual run: the `ble` set (`--no-default-features --features ble`, the S140 SoftDevice build, mutually exclusive with the default `single-core-cs` per [§ 210](#210-tier-1-ble-s140-softdevice-is-a-compile-verified-feature-gated-build--mutually-exclusive-with-the-sim-off-by-default)) and the sim set (`sim-autostart,sim-buttons,sim-course,dev-blink`, what `bin/watch-sim.sh` actually builds). The job now builds **and** runs `clippy -D warnings` against all three.

This was not hypothetical: the `ble` build had already drifted. It emitted `warning: constant FRAME_GAP is never used`, which `-D warnings` would have failed had anything run it. The root cause was not dead code — `FRAME_GAP` *is* used by `settings_rx`, and deleting it would have broken the default build. `main` gates its whole phone-link spawn block on `#[cfg(not(feature = "ble"))]`, so under `ble` the entire `phone` module is unreachable and rustc happened to flag the const first (the `#[embassy_executor::task]`-generated items don't trip the lint). The fix is a module-inner `#![cfg(not(feature = "ble"))]` in `tasks/phone.rs`, matching the reachability that already existed in `main`. Per-item `#[cfg]` would have left six unused imports failing the same gate.

The general rule this sets: **a feature set nobody builds in CI is not build-verified**, whatever a doc says about it. That matters more than usual here because [§ 314](#314-the-custom-watch-verification-ladder-becomes-a-four-rung-contract-and-tier-1-bench-verification-gets-a-checklist--neither-changes--82s-dod)'s ladder makes *build-verified* a claimable rung with named evidence, and the `ble` path can never climb higher than it before the dev kit exists — the Renode sim cannot run the proprietary SoftDevice. Build-verification is the only automated evidence that path will ever have, so it has to be real.

Don't re-litigate by:

- **Adding a feature to `app/Cargo.toml` without adding it to the CI matrix.** An ungated feature set rots silently, exactly as `ble` did.
- **Silencing a feature-gated warning with `#[allow(dead_code)]` or an underscore rename.** Both were available for `FRAME_GAP` and both would have hidden the real finding, which was that a whole module is unreachable in that build.
- **Reading a green default build as "the firmware compiles".** It compiles *one* of three ways.

Pinning: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` § `build-firmware`; the canonical command list lives in [`apps/custom_watch/local_testing.md`](../../apps/custom_watch/local_testing.md) § CI parity.
