**Decided (2026-07-26).** The run-view page indicator drew its thumb from two different roundings: the position from `active * WIDTH / total` at full precision, the width from a separately truncated `WIDTH / total`. That leaves `WIDTH - total * (WIDTH / total)` track columns owned by no page, and one of them is always the rightmost — so at the live 33-page cycle on the 168 px panel, columns 55, 111 and 167 were dead and **the last page of the ring stopped a pixel short of the right edge**. "The next tap wraps" is the one thing a position bar says better than any label could, and it read identically to the page before it. The thumb is now the half-open segment `[active * track_w / total, (active + 1) * track_w / total)`, taking its width from the same division as its position, so the enabled pages partition the track and the first and last thumbs are flush at both edges at every count. The delta is three pixels.

**What generalises is the failure shape, not the fix.** The property held at 12, 3 and 2 enabled pages because each of those divides 168 — which is to say at every count anyone had ever previewed. Sweeping 1..=64, only the fourteen divisors of 168 put the last thumb flush right. A geometry that is correct only at counts sharing a factor with the panel width is a latent bug waiting for a page to be added, and page 33 was that page.

**The redesign was rejected on arithmetic, not taste**, which is the other half worth recording. At 33 pages the thumb is a 5x3-pixel block: 0.77 x 0.46 mm at the panel's derived pitch (34.036 mm diagonal / 221.269 px = 0.1538 mm/px), subtending 6.6 x 4.0 arcmin at a 400 mm wrist glance — roughly six times the acuity limit — and its 33 positions never collide (the `.max(2)` width floor cannot engage below 85 pages). The bar was legible and honest; only its rounding was wrong. A compact numeric `7/33` fails the same arithmetic: the band is four pixels tall, a 3x4 micro-digit subtends 4.0 x 5.3 arcmin, under the character-identification floor, and the legible 8x16 face would cost a data row on every run page. Cluster-grouped ticks were rejected because the filtered mask makes them ragged in a quantifiable way — on a typical unsynced no-course run the whole synced-training and synced-summaries clusters clear, so two of five group ticks render empty — and because it would duplicate § 286's grouping somewhere it can drift from the enum.

The arithmetic moved out of `watch_render`'s drawing code into a host-tested `watch_core::statusbar::page_thumb` per § 216 (the widget had been making real geometry decisions that nothing host-tested), pinned over every page count the `u64` mask can reach, plus a `watch_render` assertion that each of the 168 columns is owned by exactly one page. The preview harness gained an **undownsampled** dump of the four-pixel band, because `ascii_dump` halves both axes and hides precisely the single-pixel seams the band is made of — the harness could not have caught this.

Don't re-litigate by:

- **Reverting to a numeric or a fill-fraction indicator.** Both were measured and both lose to the thumb; the numbers are above.
- **Deriving the thumb width from its own division again.** That is the defect.
- **Judging this widget from `ascii_dump`.** It downsamples away the feature.
- **Assuming a geometry that previews correctly is correct.** It previewed correctly at three counts, all divisors of the panel width.

## 338. Empty watch-face states speak one vocabulary, classified by what the runner can do about it

**Decided (2026-07-26).** The face's honesty rule — a surface with no data says so rather than rendering zeros a runner would read as a measurement — was well kept in behaviour and badly kept in words. A survey found a dozen spellings across thirty-odd empty states: `NOT SYNCED` on 22 pages, `NO GOAL SET` on two, `NO CUTOFFS` / `NO ROADBOOK` / `NO FUEL PLAN` / `NO GEAR SYNCED` / `NO COURSE` / `NO COURSE LOADED` on one each, and `NO ELEVATION` used on two pages for two genuinely different situations. A runner met `NO CUTOFFS` on one page and `NO COURSE` on the next with no way to know they meant the same thing.

`core/src/unfed.rs` owns the vocabulary as a nine-variant enum, and the classes are cut by **what the runner can do** rather than by which subsystem is missing, because that is the only distinction the wording has to carry: `PhoneFed` (act on the phone — `NOT SYNCED` plus the `SET VIA PHONE SYNC` remedy), `Sensor` (wait — `AWAITING BARO` / `AWAITING FIX`), `RunGate` (run on — `NEED 1 KM` / `NEED DISTANCE`), `Settled` (nothing to do; the page is fed and the answer is honestly none — `NO RACE BAND`, `NO CUTOFF AHEAD`, `LAST AID PASSED`). The remedy is **derived from the class** rather than passed per call, so a sensor or settled state cannot acquire a phone-sync instruction it has no business giving.

**Collapsing the phone-fed spellings is a correctness fix, not only a consistency one.** The watch observes an absent field and nothing more; it cannot distinguish "never configured on the phone" from "configured but not yet pushed". `NO GOAL SET` and `NO CUTOFFS` both asserted a cause the firmware has no way to know — the same class of over-claim the rest of the face avoids (`EST 220H` for an unmeasured projection, `STALE` for an aged fix, a blank battery rather than a confident 0 %). One `NOT SYNCED` says exactly what is true. Two states that had shared `NO ELEVATION` are separated for the same reason: the run's own page says `AWAITING BARO`, where `NO ELEVATION` read as an assertion that the run is flat, and a course pushed without per-point elevation says `NO COURSE ELEV` — settled, because the course *is* synced.

The abstraction is deliberately the smallest thing that makes the vocabulary enforceable rather than documented — an enum, three `const fn`s, a register, and one writer — which is the case the project's "three similar lines beat a premature helper" rule carves out at thirty-plus call sites with a cross-page invariant. It is not a templating layer: absent *values* inside an otherwise-fed row keep the `--` marker, and per-enum verdict words keep their own slot vocabulary. Drift is pinned by an invariant test whose `declared_unfed` table is **exhaustive over `Page`**, so a new page cannot compile until its empty state is classified, plus a sweep for empty-state-shaped wording outside the register; both failure paths were mutation-verified. The pass also found an untested rendering bug — `write!(rows[6], "{:<7}SYNC", "ROLLING")` rendered `ROLLINGSYNC`, a seven-character label padded to seven.

Don't re-litigate by:

- **Restoring a page-specific spelling because it reads better on that page.** The value is that all thirty read the same; a local improvement is a global regression.
- **Asserting a cause the firmware cannot observe.** `NO GOAL SET` is a guess about the phone's state.
- **Giving a Sensor or Settled state a phone-sync remedy.** The class derives the hint precisely so that cannot happen.
- **Routing an absent value through the reason vocabulary.** `HR --` is a value cell, not an empty state.

## 339. The hero band picks its face from the hero's glyphs, not from a page list

**Decided (2026-07-26).** § 292's generated numeral typography reached exactly two pages, and the reason was structural rather than an oversight: the 32x48 hero is **three rows tall**, and only the Distance/Pace glance reserves rows 0-2 (its label and state tag live on row 3). All 31 other hero-bearing pages write a label on row 2, and the hero composes after the rows, so the taller band would erase it. Rather than leave fifteen single-metric heroes pixel-doubled from the 8x16 text font, the 16x32 medium face already generated for the mixed hero's decimals becomes a hero face in its own right: the same cell size as `draw_text_2x`, so geometry, state-tag clearance and the zero-flush-at-rest contract are unchanged, but the strokes are natively rasterised bold curves rather than 2-px doubled blocks — pinned by a test asserting more ink at identical geometry, which is § 292's argument at the size these pages can afford.

**The face is chosen from the hero string's glyphs, not from a page list**, and that is the load-bearing decision. A glyph the faces lack *advances blank*, so a page list is one careless entry away from a hero that silently loses a character — and the signed Pacer and cut-off margins are exactly that hazard, since the numeral set carries no `+`. Losing the sign on the page whose whole purpose is ahead-versus-behind is the failure the `gen_font.py` `+` repair already fixed once, when a thin stem vanished and `+` packed byte-identical to `-`. Those two pages stay in the text font with their signs intact. Their honest inactive `--` *is* spellable and does take the numeral face; that split is pinned deliberately rather than special-cased, because the glyph rule self-heals — the day a regeneration adds `+`, both states converge with no page list to update.

**Two follow-ups are recorded rather than silently deferred.** Giving these pages the three-row 32x48 treatment requires moving fifteen glance bodies' row-2 labels to row 3 — worth doing, not bundled here. And **the bignum generator is not currently reproducible**: it rasterises Adobe Source Code Pro *Bold*, but the only Homebrew-installable build is the *variable* font, whose default instance is ExtraLight (1-2 px hairlines against the committed 7 px stems); instancing at `wght=700` still disagrees with the committed table on 11 of 13 glyphs in the 32x48 face and 12 of 13 in the 16x32, at 35 px ink height against the committed 34. Regenerating on such a machine would silently reshape all 26 committed glyphs into a different font build under cover of "adding a glyph". **The static face must be pinned — vendored beside the generator or an exact documented package version — before any bignum regeneration, including the one that would add `+`.**

Don't re-litigate by:

- **Dispatching the hero face on the page instead of the glyphs.** A missing glyph advances blank; the page list is the hazard.
- **Routing a signed hero to the numeral face before `+` exists.** It deletes the sign.
- **Rendering the sign small and the magnitude large.** Shrinking the safety-critical character below the number it qualifies is the wrong trade.
- **Regenerating the bignum tables without pinning the static font first.** The diff would read as one new glyph and be twenty-six reshaped ones.

## 340. A run recovered from a mid-run checkpoint is announced on the wrist; a live run's checkpoints are not

**Decided (2026-07-26).** § 316 made unfinished blobs unadvertised because a run *currently being written* must never be served: a phone could pull a torn prefix, mark it synced, and later see the same `run_seq` re-advertised at a different size. That reasoning is about **liveness, not about the flag** — at boot no run is live, so any unfinished blob on flash is terminal, orphaned by the reset that created it, and surfacing it is the entire purpose of checkpointing. `SlotDir::from_recovered` accordingly already promoted every survivor to finished, and the phone's `sim_watch_sync.dart` already ingests a blob with `FLAG_FINISHED` clear rather than refusing the only copy of an interrupted run. **The data path was already correct; the gap was that nothing told the runner.** After a brown-out the idle face looked exactly like a normal boot, and BTN1 started a fresh run with no hint that a partial one was sitting in a slot waiting to sync.

The boundary is enforced **structurally rather than by a runtime flag**: `from_recovered` is a constructor, called once from `RunStore::new()` before the record task exists, and flash is never re-scanned afterwards. A live run's checkpoints only ever pass through `reserve_checkpoint`, which hard-codes unfinished, so a run started after the boot promotion cannot inherit it however many checkpoints it writes. A slot now also records whether its bytes are a checkpoint rather than a commit — set only where a run ends without one (the boot scan, and a failed commit, so the live directory reports what a reboot would rebuild) — and `pending_partial_count()` counts the ones the phone has not pulled. The home face carries it as a standing right-anchored tag under the clock that retires itself as each run syncs. Pinned in both directions, including a property over arbitrary checkpoint/commit interleavings asserting a live run never becomes a pending partial, and a composite test that a run started after a reboot inherits nothing.

**BTN1 is deliberately unchanged** — no guard, no dismiss, no confirm. Starting a run is the most load-bearing gesture on the device and must not be gated behind dismissing a prompt at a trailhead; the honest marker plus the existing sync path is sufficient. The residual risk — with all four slots holding unsynced runs, a new run's checkpoints evict the oldest — is the documented eviction victim rule (which already sacrifices synced runs first) and a tier-2 external-flash capacity problem, not a reason to make the start gesture worse.

Don't re-litigate by:

- **Gating BTN1 behind acknowledging the pending run.** The rare case does not justify degrading the one gesture that must always work.
- **Advertising a live run's checkpoints because boot-recovered ones are advertised.** The distinction is liveness, and it is structural — do not add a runtime flag that can be got wrong.
- **Adding a partial flag to the manifest wire format.** The header's `FLAG_FINISHED` already conveys it and the phone already reads it; the watch's own bit is RAM-only, like `synced`.

## 341. The page grid states its own button map and names the cursor page — a modal that remaps buttons must not do it silently

**Decided (2026-07-26).** § 288 / § 289's hold-to-open page grid is the **fourth** button mapping on the device (idle / live run / frozen review / grid) and was the only one undiscoverable from the screen: BTN1 stops meaning pause and drives the cursor, BTN2 stops arming the stop and cancels, and the title row printed only `B4 GO` — the one role that least needed explaining. A runner who over-holds BTN3 with cold hands finds the two-press emergency stop replaced by cancel-then-two-presses, discovered only by trying. On a device with no haptics at hour 60, a modal that lies about its buttons is the defect. Separately the grid committed a jump — on BTN4 or the 3 s auto-select — off a four-glyph code alone, and four glyphs cannot separate 33 pages.

The grid now spends two of its nine text rows saying what it is: row 0 the button legend, row 1 the cursor page's full name (longest `ELEVATION PROFILE`, 17 of 21 cells, fit and uniqueness test-pinned). **Button semantics are untouched** — they were reasoned about and were never the bug; `core/src/button.rs` needed zero edits.

**The legend names BTN2 and BTN4 only, and the asymmetry is the decision.** A full four-button row fits at exactly 21 cells with zero slack and was rejected: BTN1/BTN3 move a visible cursor and commit nothing, so a runner discovers them for one harmless press, whereas **BTN2's remap is the safety surprise and the one press that cannot reveal itself** — the grid closes identically whether or not the stop armed. `B2 EXIT` names the route back to where BTN2 stops, and the run view's `STOP? BTN2` banner picks up the chain on the other side. Cramming to the last cell on a 1-bit reflective panel read by headlamp is also the opposite of glanceable.

**Renaming the confusable codes behind a minimum-edit-distance test was considered and rejected on measurement.** Over all 528 pairs the minimum Levenshtein is 1, at exactly `LOAD`/`ROAD` and `PACE`/`PACR` — but a ≥2 floor would *pass* `REDY`/`RDAY` (a transposition) and `PACR`/`RCAP` (an anagram), the very pairs the review flagged, while forcing churn on the two it does catch; a ≥3 floor needs most of the 24 distance-2 pairs re-cut, and trading a mnemonic abbreviation for a Hamming-distant one spends the recognisability that is itself the defence. The root cause is not that two codes are close, it is that a four-glyph code was **load-bearing at commit time**. With the name row it is a position marker and nothing commits off it, so the codes stand.

The rows are affordable only because of § 333: 33 codes at four columns need `ceil(33/4)` = 9 rows and the panel has exactly 9, so both chrome rows come out of body capacity (32 → 28 cells) and full-mask scroll depth goes 1 → 2, while the everyday ~12-page mask still never scrolls. Before § 333 made the body a cursor-keyed window this would have tripped its `const` capacity assert. The cursor row cannot be displaced by construction, and a resting grid still flushes zero lines.

Don't re-litigate by: **naming all four buttons for symmetry** (the two that self-reveal do not need it, and the row loses its air); **renaming codes behind an edit-distance floor** (the metric misses the transpositions that caused the complaint); or **reclaiming a chrome row for body capacity** (the name row is what stops a jump committing off a confusable code).

## 342. The glyph generators rasterise a vendored, digest-pinned font face — and the pin proved the tables were reproducible all along

**Decided (2026-07-26). Corrects § 339's diagnosis while keeping its caution.** § 339 recorded the numeral tables as unreproducible and forbade regenerating them until the source face was pinned. The face is now pinned by **vendoring the exact static OTFs** from `adobe-fonts/source-code-pro` under `drivers/sharp_mip/fonts/`, beside the OFL 1.1 text that clause 2 requires accompany a redistributed copy — licence confirmed both from `LICENSE.md` at the vendored tag and from the OTF's own `name` table, not from a webpage.

Vendoring beat "pin a package version plus a fetch script" for one reason worth stating flatly: **the name of a face does not determine its bytes.** `-font Source-Code-Pro-Bold` resolved to a different weight on one machine and to nothing at all on another. A path plus a SHA256 determines the bytes; a family name never can. `scripts/pinned_face.py` verifies the digest before either generator draws a pixel, so a wrong face fails loudly instead of silently reshaping a table — proved by substituting ExtraLight and watching it refuse.

**The pin's first job was to answer whether the committed tables were ever reproducible, and they were.** `bignum.rs` and `font.rs` both regenerate byte-for-byte (the latter after the `cargo fmt` pass it already carries), at the committed 34 px / 17 px ink heights, and all three static releases agree at these cell sizes. § 339's 11-of-13 and 12-of-13 disagreements and its 35 px measurement were **entirely an artifact of instancing the variable build at `wght=700`**, not a release difference. The tables were never wrong — only unverifiable. That distinction matters for how the earlier entry is read.

With that settled, adding `+` became a reviewable one-glyph change: the diff removes three lines (the glyph-set literal and two table arities) and leaves **all 26 existing bitmaps byte-identical**, which is itself the evidence the pin worked. Collision-freedom is proved, not assumed — a test asserts `+` inks rows the dash leaves empty in **both** faces, because the precedent failure was a `+` whose stem vanished and packed byte-identical to `-`; a different-bitmap assertion would not have caught that. `+`/`-` is the closest pair in each table, at 114 and 20 bits.

**The convergence then cost one byte.** `NUMERAL_GLYPHS` gained `+`; because § 339 dispatches the hero face on glyph coverage rather than a page list, Pacer and CutoffEta promoted off the text font with **no page list edited and no change to `app/src/tasks/ui.rs`**. § 339's self-healing property is now demonstrated rather than argued, and those pages' inactive `--` and live `+0:42` finally render in the same face.

Two things are deliberately not claimed: **`icons.rs` reproduction is unverified** (Inkscape is absent on the authoring machine, though its SVG inputs were always vendored — only the rasteriser is unpinned, and the generator now says so and names a missing tool), and nothing here is sim- or bench-verified.

**Follow-up, now unblocked rather than deferred:** a CI step that regenerates both tables and diffs them — the firmware equivalent of `gen:types:check`. It was impossible while the face came from the machine's font set. It should land **non-gating first**, because the *rasteriser* version is still unpinned and a version skew would otherwise red every unrelated PR.

Don't re-litigate by: **naming a face by fontconfig family again** (that is the whole defect); **regenerating when the digest check fails** (restore the pinned face, or land a deliberate re-baseline as its own reviewable commit); or **reading "reproducible" as CI-enforced** — it is not, yet.

## 343. A timed press tier announces itself before it fires

**Decided (2026-07-26).** BTN3 on a run view carries three tiers: a tap pages forward, a release between 0.5 s and 1.5 s pages back, a hold past 1.5 s opens the page grid. The grid tier fires while held, so the grid appearing is its own feedback — but the boundary *into* page-back had none, and neither did the escalation window above it. A cold, gloved thumb at hour 60 has degraded proprioception for exactly "how long have I been pressing this", so the two press-classification boundaries most exposed to the conditions the device exists for were the two that said nothing. And the failure is not merely confusing: over-holding lands the runner in the modal § 341 describes.

Past the first threshold the hero band carries an inverse-video `GRID? HOLD` banner for as long as the button is down, reusing the armed-stop prompt's exact treatment and its `<outcome>? <how>` grammar. It is **discrete rather than a progress bar, and it names the next tier rather than the current one**: the tier already earned is what releasing gives you, so the only actionable information is "keep holding and you get the grid". One banner carries three facts — the button is registering, you are past the first threshold, more holding escalates. That is what the **overshoot** case needs, and the overshoot is the expensive outcome; the undershoot (release early, get page-next) is cheap and self-correcting. A continuous countdown would optimise for the cheap failure at four or five panel flushes where this costs two `Watch` sends.

**The prompt is driven entirely by the press, and the no-standing-waker property is structural.** The hardware task raises the flag on entry to the escalation `select` it was *already* awaiting and lowers it however that select resolves, including a release lost in the re-arm gap; a tap never reaches the threshold and costs zero sends. Critically `state::BTN3_HOLD` carries **no timestamp and no TTL** — unlike `STOP_ARMED`, which stores `armed_at_s` — so it cannot enter the screen task's `owes_timed_refresh` decision and cannot create the standing wake § 328 removed. A resting face keeps its 30 s heartbeat and flushes zero SPI.

Ranking: armed-stop banner > hold prompt > alert banner > page hero, with the grid drawn over everything. On Distance / Pace the three-row numeral hero stands down via the same `hero_band` input the armed stop already uses. The idle face gets no prompt at all — an idle hold is the § 290 QNH re-zero, so there is no second tier and naming one would be a lie; the predicate derives from `btn3_action` rather than the state, so it cannot advertise a grid on a surface without one.

**The thresholds stay at 500 ms / 1500 ms.** 500 ms is the long-press default of both phone platforms (Android `DEFAULT_LONG_PRESS_TIMEOUT`, iOS `minimumPressDuration`), so a gloved thumb arrives already trained on it, and it is 25x the task's 20 ms debounce, which is what stops contact bounce promoting a tap; the grid tier sits a further full second on. No citable gloved-press measurement was available and none was invented. The better argument is structural: **the problem was never the absolute values but that the gap between them was invisible.** With the window announced, the grid hold becomes a feedback-controlled gesture rather than an open-loop timed one, and the precision demanded drops to "see the prompt, then decide". A test pins both values and the ratio so a future change argues with this reasoning.

**The grid's 3 s auto-select is deliberately left without a countdown**, recorded as a known gap rather than a TODO: this prompt rides a timer the press already owns, whereas a countdown inside an open modal needs a per-second wake for its whole duration — the § 328 shape.

Don't re-litigate by: **making it a countdown** (optimises for the cheap failure and costs flushes); **naming the current tier instead of the next** (the current tier is what releasing already gives you); **giving `BTN3_HOLD` a TTL** (that is how it acquires a standing waker); or **retuning the thresholds without evidence** — the gap was the bug, not the numbers.

## 344. The required CI gate carries the proven sim scenario, not the whole sim job

**Decided (2026-07-26).** The Renode `sim-firmware` job was deliberately outside the `CI gate` aggregator's `needs:` list because it had never executed on a hosted runner. It has now run green repeatedly, so the exclusion is stale — but promoting the job wholesale would make the `pages` and `alerts` scenarios blocking across the entire monorepo **two runs after they first executed**, which is precisely the flake risk the original comment warned about. Being newly green is not the same as having a flake history.

So the job is split rather than promoted. `sim-firmware` runs `smoke` — the sequence with the 2026-07-19 manual verification pass behind it and a long green record — and joins the gate. A new `sim-scenarios` job carries `pages` + `alerts`, **strict within itself** so a regression fails loudly and visibly, but not required until it has run green over a stretch of unrelated PRs. The cost is one extra Renode install per run; the buy is a required signal that is actually proven rather than merely recent.

The two jobs write their artifacts to separate subdirectories under one uploaded parent, which is not cosmetic: `ci_smoke.py` unlinks its `sim-output.log` / `frame.ppm` / pointer on start, so scenarios sharing an out-dir would each destroy the previous one's evidence — the exact opposite of what a failure artifact is for.

Don't re-litigate by: **promoting `sim-scenarios` because it is green today** (wait for history across unrelated PRs); **merging the jobs back to save a Renode install** (the required gate would then rest on the newest assertions); or **making the scenario steps `continue-on-error`** (a silently tolerated regression is worse than an unrequired loud one).

## 345. Hero size follows what a page's body can spare, and a hero too wide for the tall face drops to the medium one

**Decided (2026-07-26).** § 339 gave every numeral hero a generated face but reached the 32x48 one on exactly two pages, for a structural reason it recorded as a follow-up: that face is three rows tall and only the Distance / Pace glances reserve rows 0-2. The follow-up estimated fifteen row-2 labels to move. The real number is **seven**. The other pages cannot: the zones, splits, roadbook, predictor and training-paces bodies fill rows 3..7 with a ladder, the pacer and back-to-start pages label row 3, and the fuel, gear and elevation pages hand row 3 (or rows 3..8) to a `watch_render` overlay. Row 2 is the only row those bodies have.

So the rule is not a curated list of favourites but `face::body_top_row(page)` — matched exhaustively over `Page`, so a new page cannot compile until it is classified, and pinned against the builders by `every_page_leaves_its_hero_band_blank`. That test is the point of the design: a page that claimed three rows and then wrote a header on row 2 would have it silently erased by the hero drawn over it, and nothing else reads those cells.

The seven promoted pages move their header to row 3 with the state tag beside it, which is where the two existing tall pages have carried theirs since § 292. Three of them tightened a label's padding to clear the tag's cells; `the_state_tag_survives_on_every_page` asserts the refuse-rather-than-truncate write never actually has to refuse, so a header that grows into those cells fails the suite rather than dropping the recording indicator on the wrist.

Promoting more pages made a latent hole load-bearing. `draw_bignum_hero` **drops glyphs past the right edge**, so an over-wide hero does not overflow — it silently loses its last digits. On a cut-off margin (`+10:05:30` renders `+10:05:3`) that is a wrong number displayed as confidently as a right one. `ui_frame::tall_hero_fits` budgets the hero in text cells — four per big glyph, two per medium, pinned against the driver's real tables in the preview beside the existing glyph-set pin — and falls back to the medium face when it does not fit. **Smaller and whole beats larger and truncated**, which is the same call § 339 made when it kept a signed hero in the text font rather than advance a blank cell.

Don't re-litigate by: **promoting a page whose body needs row 2** (the header goes under the hero, invisibly — that is what the invariant test exists to catch); **budgeting the fit in pixels** (`watch_core` would have to learn the panel's width, which is the driver's business); or **letting a wide hero truncate because the everyday values fit** (the values that overflow are the multi-day ones, which is the device's whole premise).

## 346. The run view gets a battery marker, and the standing-marker row stops being clipped by the hero

**Decided (2026-07-26).** § 294 put the supply rail on the face and gated it to the idle views — icon on the home face, `BAT n%` row on diagnostics — with the ui task commenting that "run views carry neither." That was a deliberate placement decision at the time, but it leaves a device built for 100-hour efforts, whose GNSS mode picker exists purely to trade fixes for hours, with **no way to learn the cell is going without stopping the run**. Every other standing condition on the wrist has a marker; the one the runner can least afford to be surprised by did not.

It now shares the fuel-overdue marker row, with the precedence stated in one place rather than left to call order: **critical cell > fuel reminder > low cell**. A sip can wait a kilometre. A watch that dies ends the recording, and the remedy — drop to Expedition at the next stop, reach the power bank in the drop bag — needs lead time. Between the two thresholds the fuel state is the more actionable, and the battery tag returns the moment the reminder is acknowledged. `battery::CRITICAL_PCT` is the discharge-curve anchor below the knee (3.68 V, 380 mV above the cutoff at which a LiPo damages itself), derived the same way `LOW_PCT` is the knee itself — not a round number chosen for looking like one.

Adding a second tenant surfaced that the row's existing one was already broken. The hero is drawn **after** the text rows and composes its span from scratch, so it erases whatever it overlaps, and the fuel marker's doc comment had assumed that away: "the hero digits sit to its left, so the small right-anchored tag never collides with them at glanceable elapsed times." Past ten hours that is false. A nine-glyph elapsed hero spans eighteen of the twenty-one cells and ate the tag's first two characters, leaving `INK` — and ultra-length elapsed times are the device's design case, not an edge. `ui_frame::hero_row_cells` reports the span per band and the marker refuses when it cannot clear it, the same refuse-rather-than-truncate rule the state tag follows.

That clearance rule is also why the battery form is a bare `12%` rather than `BAT 12%`: three cells is what survives a 100-hour hero, and a seven-cell tag would be refused precisely on the runs where the cell is the thing at stake. It is unambiguous where it sits — the only other tenants of that row are words.

Residual, recorded rather than papered over: the five-cell fuel tag is now **absent** past a nine-glyph hero where it used to be mangled. Absent is the honest state and the reminder still gets its transient inverse banner — this row is only its standing backstop — but a shorter fuel vocabulary would recover it, and that is a wire-visible wording change worth its own pass.

Bench-gated like the rest of § 294: the USB-powered DK publishes no plausible cell, so the marker cannot appear in Renode and its rendering is host-tested only.

## 347. maplibre-gl v6 is ESM-only with no default export, and it drops WebGL 1 — the map now requires WebGL 2

**Decided (2026-07-27).** maplibre-gl 6.0.0 stops publishing the UMD bundles (`maplibre-gl.js`, `maplibre-gl-csp.js`) and ships only `dist/maplibre-gl.mjs`, whose exports are all named — there is no `default`. Every one of our seven map surfaces did `import maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl'`, so the bump alone failed the build with seven `[MISSING_EXPORT] "default" is not exported` errors before a single test ran. The fix is the namespace form, `import * as maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl'`, plus `import type * as maplibregl` in `map_resize.ts`; `maplibre-gl/dist/maplibre-gl.css` is unchanged and still resolves, because v6 keeps `"./dist/*"` in its exports map.

**The consequence that isn't in the diff: v6 requires WebGL 2.** WebGL 1 support is gone, so a browser or device that can only do WebGL 1 now gets no map at all rather than a degraded one. Every map surface is a layer-2 concern under the layered-resilience contract, so this costs the map, not the run — but it is a real narrowing of the device floor and is the reason this bump is worth an entry rather than being a routine dependency bump.

**The break that the build could not see: v6 loads its worker from a URL it computes at runtime.** Dropping the UMD bundles also dropped the inlined worker. v6 instead does `new URL('./maplibre-gl-worker.mjs', import.meta.url)` — and because that specifier is assembled from a variable rather than written as a static literal, no bundler can see it as an asset reference. After bundling, `import.meta.url` is the emitting chunk's URL, so it resolves to a path under `_app/immutable/chunks/` that Vite never writes. The worker 404s, no tile is ever parsed, and the map simply never fires `idle`. Nothing fails loudly: the build is green, the page renders, the map is blank. That is what made this the expensive half of the bump — twelve e2e specs (heatmap clustering, pin popups, hover-preview, course-marker drag) all failed on `data-map-idle="true"` never attaching or `querySourceFeatures` returning nothing, which reads as twelve unrelated UI bugs rather than one missing file.

The fix is `apps/web/src/lib/routes/maplibre.ts`: a single module that imports the worker with Vite's `?worker&url`, calls `setWorkerUrl` with the emitted asset, and re-exports the namespace. Every map surface imports the engine from there, so a new call site cannot silently skip the wiring. `?worker&url` rather than a plain `?url` because the worker is a **module** worker that imports its sibling `maplibre-gl-shared.mjs` — a one-file copy leaves that import dangling. Verified on both paths, since they differ and the e2e suite exercises the dev one: the production build emits `_app/immutable/workers/maplibre-gl-worker-*.js` (self-contained, no `maplibre-gl-shared` references) and references it from the map chunk, and `vite dev` serves the real 131 KB worker through `?worker_file&type=module`.

That self-containment is what costs the bundle budget 126 KB gzipped, so the ceiling moves 2200 → 2400 in the same change: the shared style/tile-parsing code is now on disk twice, once in the map chunk and once in the worker, where v5's inline UMD worker counted it once. Measured total 2196 KB — the old ceiling technically passed, with 4 KB of noise-level headroom that would have flapped on the next PR. De-duplicating it needs a self-hosted worker + shared pair and belongs to the bundle-trim pass, not here.

Two things the migration checked but did **not** have to change, recorded so the next person doesn't re-derive them: nothing in the app touches the APIs v6 actually removed or renamed — no `map.transform`, no `styleimagemissing` handler, no `MapLibreZoomEvent` / `MapDataEvent` — and every `GeoJSONSource.setData()` call already passed one argument, so losing the second (`waitForCompletion`) parameter is a no-op for us.

The one type-level break was `geolocate.on('error', …)`, whose parameter is now `GeolocateErrorEvent` rather than the DOM's `GeolocationPositionError`. The handler only reads `err.code`, which `GeolocateErrorEvent` still carries, so the annotation was deleted rather than retyped — inference off the control's typed event map is what stops the same annotation going stale on the next bump.

A note on measuring this, because the obvious local check misleads: `pnpm run check` reports ~37 `Cannot find namespace 'GeoJSON'` errors that have nothing to do with maplibre. `@types/geojson` is a dependency of v5 **and** v6; npm hoists it to the root `node_modules/@types` and TypeScript's automatic type inclusion finds it, while pnpm's strict layout leaves it under `.pnpm/` where it doesn't. Installing v5 into a pnpm tree reproduces all 37, so they are a package-manager layout artifact, not a regression. CI does not run `svelte-check` at all (only `check:check-constraints`), which is why the noise has never surfaced there.

## 348. The GPS gap re-anchor asks two clocks, so a bad device clock can't freeze distance for the rest of the run

The `#330` re-anchor (see [run_recording.md § GPS pipeline](../features/run_recording.md)) is the escape hatch that stops a stale anchor freezing distance: when a hop fails the < 100 m one-hop cap but a genuine interval has elapsed, the recorder rebases onto the fresh fix without crediting the un-sampled gap. It gated that "genuine interval" question on `dt` derived from `Position.timestamp` — GPS-reported time — deliberately, so that a zero-dt duplicate could not slip a teleport past the speed clamp.

That gate is unreachable exactly when it is most needed. `dt` is `pos.timestamp.difference(lastAt)`, so a device clock that jumps **backwards** — an NTP correction, a manual time change, a phone that boots with a bad clock and then syncs — leaves `lastAt` in the future. Every subsequent fix then computes a non-positive `dt`, which the clamp reads as implausible *and* which is below the re-anchor window. Both branches fail, the anchor never moves, and distance stays frozen until real time catches back up past the anchor — bounded only by the size of the jump. A clock that **stalls** (every fix carrying the same timestamp) froze it outright, with no bound at all. In both cases the elapsed clock stays correct, because that has been `Stopwatch`-based since the start; it is only distance that is exposed.

The fix is to ask the monotonic clock the same question and let either answer fire the rebase: alongside `_lastTrackedPositionAt` the anchor now stamps `_lastTrackedElapsed` from the same `_stopwatch` that already backs elapsed, and the escape fires on `dt >= 10 s || monotonicGap >= 10 s`. A `Stopwatch` cannot go backwards or stall, so the gap it measures grows with real recording time whatever the timestamps do — which is what makes the escape *unconditionally* self-healing rather than self-healing-if-the-clock-is-sane.

The reason this cannot weaken the teleport guard is worth stating, because it is the whole objection to touching this code: the monotonic arm only fires where GPS time claims a **shorter** gap than the monotonic clock — that is, precisely where GPS time is the untrustworthy input. A corrupt fix arriving immediately after a good one has a short gap on *both* clocks and still fails closed. Both must agree the gap is short for a hop to be rejected, which is a strictly narrower rejection condition than "GPS time says so".

Two smaller consequences. A stalled clock now keeps the **track** growing (the path is still recorded) while still crediting no distance — speed is unverifiable with a dt of zero, so failing closed on distance is right, but failing closed on the track as well was losing the run's shape for no benefit. And the three anchor fields are now treated as one unit: the tracking block takes the fresh-anchor branch if *any* of them is null, so a future divergence between them re-anchors rather than freezing — the same fail-toward-self-heal posture as the rest of the change.

`RunRecorder` gained an optional `clock` constructor parameter for this. It exists solely so tests can drive the monotonic gap without waiting out ten real seconds; production takes the default. The four new cases in `run_recorder_test.dart` pin the backwards jump, the stalled clock, the guarantee that no timestamp sequence strands the anchor, and — the mirror of that guarantee — that a teleport with no real time elapsed is still rejected.

The `apps/custom_watch` port of this filter chain (`core/src/record.rs`) was never exposed: it measures `dt` from `Fix::uptime_s`, a device uptime counter that is monotonic by construction. No change was needed there, and it is the same shape this change gives the Dart side.

## 349. The sim's clickable buttons sit at their §81 Fenix positions, not in a strip under the panel

The Renode display model's BTN1–BTN4 boxes were a horizontal strip under the LCD — functional, but it trains the wrong muscle memory: on the watch itself ([§ 81](#81-custom-watch-input-is-5-physical-buttons-in-the-garmin-fenix-layout-no-touchscreen)) the buttons flank the case. `sim/SharpMipDisplay.cs` now draws the four boxes in bezel strips either side of the panel, each at the §81 slot its tier-1 function stands in for: BTN1 upper-right (START/STOP), BTN4 lower-right (BACK/LAP), BTN3 lower-left (the DOWN slot, matching its page-down role), BTN2 mid-left (the UP slot — the least-wrong home for stop, whose true Fenix home, START, is already BTN1's), and the left-top LIGHT slot deliberately empty because the DK has only four buttons and tier 1 has no backlight. Pin wiring, the `btnN` macros, and `DumpFrame` (panel-only by design) are untouched — this is analyzer-window chrome only, verified by driving all four boxes through the pointer path in a headless sim (every box reached its gpio0 pin and the firmware reacted).

## 350. Paging is spatial — the left button pages left, the right button pages right, and the lap moves to a fifth button

**Decided (2026-07-27), owner-driven.** The run-view page ring renders *horizontally* (the §-invariant top-edge position thumb), but the press grammar walked it asymmetrically: tap forward, 0.5 s long-press backward — which the owner read in the sim as "I can only navigate right" even after §290 gave `FIN` a tap-back. The industry idiom doesn't help here: Garmin pages with left-side UP/DOWN, Polar and Suunto with a right-side stack — all *vertical* metaphors, prev/next stacked on ONE side. Ours is horizontal, and stimulus-response compatibility says the control should sit where the display moves. So the grammar is now spatial: **BTN3 (lower-left, the §81 DOWN slot) tap pages LEFT and BTN4 (lower-right) tap pages RIGHT, in every run view** — recording, paused, and finished alike. The lap that BTN4 carried moves to a **new BTN5 in the §81 LIGHT slot** (upper-left; Polar precedent — lap on its own OK key), because the paging pair must stay plain taps. Tier 1 has no fifth DK button, so BTN5 is an external momentary on P0.02 (header pin, internal pull-up — unwired it idles high, a dead key rather than a phantom press); §81's five-button 3+2 *shape* is untouched, only the slot *assignments* are now ours instead of Garmin's. The press grammar collapses from three tiers to two: tap under 0.5 s, hold at 0.5 s — and the hold's action fires AT the threshold while still held, so the grid now opens a full second sooner (0.5 s, was 1.5 s) from EITHER paging key, and the middle tier plus its `GRID? HOLD` banner (§334) are deleted — the tier the banner disambiguated no longer exists. In the grid, BTN3/BTN4 move the cursor the same directions they page (tap ±1, hold ±row), **BTN1 confirms — `B1 GO`, the START-confirms idiom every five-button watch trains** — replacing §289's BTN1-cursor-back, BTN2 still cancels, BTN5 is swallowed. §289's computed press-cost table is unchanged (same move sets: worst 6, average 3.76 at 33 pages), but every action got cheaper in wall-time — backward is a tap instead of a 0.5 s hold, and §286's safety contract improves: Back-to-start is now one *tap* from home. Idle meanings stand (§291): BTN3 tap GNSS mode / hold QNH re-zero, BTN4 diagnostics toggle whatever the duration, BTN5 inert. Supersedes §290 (FIN tap-back — now the everywhere rule) and §334 (the banner); amends §289 (grid keys) and §337 (the legend reads `B2 EXIT … B1 GO`). Host-tested in `watch_core::button` + `input_flow`; sim-verified via ci_smoke (BTN4-forward walk, BTN3-tap inverse) and a pointer-click pass over all five bezel boxes.

## 351. The watch gets an idle settings menu on BTN5, speaking the grid's dialect, and every interaction is priced at its floor

**Decided (2026-07-27), owner-driven, the §350 follow-through.** Two asks: minimize presses everywhere, and give the watch an on-device settings page. On the first, [`navigation.md § Every interaction, priced`](../custom_watch/navigation.md) now inventories the whole surface: every core interaction is a single tap (start, pause/resume, lap, dismiss, page step, grid open, mode cycle, re-zero, diagnostics, settings), any of 33 pages costs at most 6 actions / 3.8 average (the §289 BFS-computed optimum for a no-chord five-key grammar; ~2.2 average under a typical curated mask), and exactly one interaction sits above its floor on purpose — the stop's two-press guard, which trades one press for not ending a 100-mile recording on a brushed sleeve. On the second: **a BTN5 tap on the idle face opens a settings menu** — the lap key is dead while idle, the same dead-key repurposing that gave `FIN` its page-back (§290) and idle BTN4 the diagnostics toggle (§291). The menu is a modal that speaks the page grid's exact dialect so nothing new has to be learned: BTN4/BTN3 step the cursor the directions they page, **BTN1 activates, BTN2 (or BTN5 again) exits, and the legend row is byte-identical to the grid's `B2 EXIT … B1 GO` (pinned by a host test)**. Three items at tier 1: **GNSS MODE** (cycles in place, projected hours readable *before* committing — the quick idle-BTN3 blind cycle stays, both routes run one shared `cycle_gnss_mode`), **HIDE EMPTY** (the §284 filter, the one curation lever that belongs on the wrist — the 33-bit per-page mask stays a phone surface), and **RE-ZERO ALTITUDE** (fires the same request as the idle BTN3 hold and hands the screen to the idle face's banner). Value items stay open — the row re-rendering with the new value IS the confirmation; the action item closes. Every press inside is swallowed (a menu can never start, pause, or lap a run), the menu is idle-only (a run starting under it closes it), and a 30 s inactivity deadline closes an abandoned menu because it covers the home clock ("the home face always tells the time") — a deadline armed per press, never a standing wake (§328). **Persistence rides CFG1's reserved byte**: bit 0 = "hide-empty explicitly chosen", bit 1 = the value — pre-§351 records decode unchanged (flags 0 = no choice) with no version bump, and the record task persists the choice *whichever side made it* (the menu's toggle and a phone's `SET1` push land on the same `state::SETTINGS` channel), so the last writer is what a reboot restores, and a repeated push never re-erases the page. Sim-verified end-to-end: open/step/activate/toggle/exit/timeout, both persist paths, restore of hide-empty **and** GNSS mode across a `machine RequestReset`, and the quick paths (BTN1 start, BTN5 mid-run lap) intact; all three ci_smoke scenarios stay green.

**Key map revised same day (owner feedback), superseding the paragraph above's borrow of the grid's dialect.** A settings list is *vertical* with a value axis *across* each row — so the keys now match that geometry instead of the grid's: **BTN2/BTN3 (the mid-left/lower-left §81 slots Garmin literally names UP and DOWN, stacked vertically on the case) move the cursor; BTN5/BTN1 (the upper-left/upper-right corners, a horizontal pair) edit the selected row — left = off/decrease, right = on/increase, right also fires the action row; BTN4 (the §81 BACK slot) exits.** Edits are *directional and idempotent*, not blind toggles: HIDE EMPTY is right=ON / left=OFF (pressing the side you want can never overshoot), and GNSS MODE is a clamped ladder — right toward Expedition (more hours), left toward Performance (more fixes), no wrap, so a press past the end cannot teleport to the opposite extreme (the idle quick tap keeps its wrap cycle; both routes share one `set_gnss_mode`). The modal dialects now deliberately diverge — the grid's cursor rides the paging pair because it walks the horizontal page ring; the menu rides the vertical pair because it walks a list — each spatially true to what it shows. The one §337-class surprise, EXIT moving from the grid's B2 to the menu's B4, is exactly what the menu's legend names: `B5- B1+       B4 EXIT`; the cursor keys move a visible marker and stay unlabelled, per §337's name-only-what-is-not-self-revealing rule. Change-a-setting cost is unchanged (open + ≤2 cursor steps + one edit press ≤ 4). Re-sim-verified: the full directional walk (down/up on BTN3/BTN2, OFF/ON on BTN5/BTN1, the ladder up to Expedition and back, re-zero on BTN1, exit on BTN4), persistence + reset-restore, quick paths, all three ci_smoke scenarios.

## 352. Rolling training load syncs whole, and the run's stress goes TRIMP once the resting HR rides SET1 v5

**2026-07-28.** Two halves of the roadmap's "Training load / acute-chronic balance" row close together, both pulled forward from tier 2 because neither needed the silicon migration nor a missing BOM part (the `tier2_scope.md` phase-4 precedent).

The **rolling CTL/ATL/TSB trio** stays phone-computed — the watch holds no multi-day history, and pioneering a second aggregation would break §24 — and lands through the `set_fitness` hook shape: a `LoadTrendView` behind a plausibility-guarded `Recorder::set_load_trend`, an honest `ROLLING NOT SYNCED` row until a push arrives, and a `CTL/ATL` + signed `FORM` render once it does. The trio is accepted or rejected **whole** (the pace-band atomicity rule): a non-finite or implausible member drops the push and the current view stands, because blending one corrupt value into two good ones would show a runner a form verdict nobody computed. Like `set_fitness` / `set_readiness` there is deliberately no wire field yet — the view setters await the stats-frame design — so the page's rolling half is host-fed until then, and honestly labelled on-device.

The **single-run stress** stops being hard-coded to the distance proxy. The recorder now banks a time-weighted HR sum exactly where zone time banks (moving seconds with a live reading — so both HR aggregates agree on which seconds carried a pulse), and `SET1` **v5** takes `flags2` bit 6 for the **resting HR** — the second half of the TRIMP calibration pair `FLAG_MAX_HR` has carried since v1. With both halves synced and an average banked, `compute_stress` runs the same Banister-TRIMP ladder the web/Dart helpers run; missing either half, or a sensorless run, stays honestly on the distance model, and the page's `LOAD` row names which model scored it (`TRIMP` / `DIST` — the web chart's "HR-based" vs "volume-based" split). `set_max_hr` now also stores the value it always guarded, `set_resting_hr` guards 25..=120 (reject-don't-clamp), and a v4 frame claiming bit 6 is rejected — a v4 encoder could never have set it. The v4 full-frame golden is frozen as a compat vector (the §293 v1→v2 drill), the Dart encoder + goldens moved in lockstep across both byte-identical twins, and the resting-HR-only vector is pinned Rust↔Dart.

## 353. Activity profiles are macros over existing knobs — a curated page mask plus a GNSS mode, applied from the menu, never a container

**2026-07-28.** The parity backlog's "Activity profiles" row (Run / Trail / Ultra / Hike, "each with its own data screens + defaults") lands at tier 1, pulled forward like §352 because everything it needs already exists: the §284/§286 curated `pages_mask`, the shared `set_gnss_mode` path, CFG1 persistence, and the §351 settings menu to select from.

A profile is deliberately a **macro, not a container**. Garmin's activity profiles are stateful containers — per-profile settings that follow the profile around. Ours applies a named preset to the SAME mutable knobs everything else writes: the pages preset rides the `state::SETTINGS` channel a phone push takes, the mode rides the shared quick-cycle path, and §351's last-writer rule then holds with no third state system — a later `SET1` pages push or an idle mode tap simply overwrites the knob it names, and the stored profile id remains honestly "last applied". The menu row is a fourth item on the §351 list (the four-item ring keeps the ≤ 2-cursor-step, ≤ 4-press bound), edited as a clamped directional ladder ordered by activity length — Run (Performance) → Trail (Balanced) → Ultra → Hike (both Expedition) — so right always reads "longer, more battery"; the first-ever right press starts at Run, and left of an unset row applies nothing (a surprise preset application is worse than a dead press). The selection persists in CFG1's reserved byte behind a third flags bit — the §351 no-version-bump drill — and boot re-applies the stored profile's page preset; `persist_hide_empty` had to stop rebuilding the flags byte from scratch for this, which is the general lesson: a shared flags byte is carried forward, never reconstructed.

Two exclusions are the decision's edges. The presets carry **no alert-cadence axis**: the fuel cadences are `fuel_plan`-derived product numbers, and per-profile physiology invented on the watch would pioneer past web (§24) — the desert case already has its wire (`SET1` `FLAG_FUEL`). And the page masks are **curation, not capability**: Run drops the pushed-course cluster, Hike drops the racing cluster, Trail/Ultra keep the full cycle and differ on GNSS cadence alone — but every preset keeps the Dashboard and Back-to-start (§286's safety page is not activity-specific), and any dropped page returns via a pages push or a different profile.

## 354. Tier-1 structured-workout execution: pushed pre-expanded steps, a lap-press skip, and a clock that pauses like the phone's

**Decided (2026-07-28).** The last big on-run-guidance gap in the parity backlog — running a planned workout (warmup → reps → recoveries → cooldown) on the wrist — lands as `watch_core::workout`, a faithful port of the mobile `WorkoutRunner` (`packages/run_recorder/lib/src/workout_runner.dart`, spec `docs/features/workout_execution.md`), per §24 a port of shipped product behaviour, not a pioneered variant. Four decisions worth recording. **(1) Steps travel pre-expanded.** `expandWorkoutSteps` needs the plan's structure + paces bag, which live on the phone — so the watch receives the flat step list over a new `WKT1` frame (`workout_store`), the roadbook's pushed-pre-built model. The frame is CRC-sealed **from v1** (the §335 reasoning: a flipped byte in a target distance is a plausible *different* workout — 400 m reps become 4496 m reps — and per-step validation cannot tell them apart), fail-closed on unknown kinds, a step with both end axes set, or an implausible target (reusing the pace-band + pacer-distance plausibility constants rather than minting new ones), and chunked over a sixth GATT characteristic through a `WorkoutAssembler` that mirrors the course assembler; the shared `offset | payload` splitter is now `ble_sync::parse_push_chunk`. The Dart encoder (`watch_workout.dart`, iOS twin byte-identical) accepts `run_recorder`'s own `WorkoutStep` type — the same objects `expandWorkoutSteps` emits — and pins the same golden vectors as the Rust tests. **(2) The lap button doubles as step-skip.** The §350 grammar has no spare button mid-run, and Garmin's own semantics make the lap press advance the workout step — so `Recorder::lap` closes the lap *and* skips the armed workout's current step. Rewind and abandon are deliberately not ported (no button budget; stopping the run or ignoring the page covers abandon), and neither is the halfway cue (a display-only banner with no chime spams the slot; the page's live progress carries it) — the end-of-step warning IS ported, as the time-critical one. **(3) The workout clock is elapsed minus manually-paused time.** The phone runner reads a stopwatch that halts on a manual pause but runs through an auto-pause — a standing rest inside a timed recovery is the step working as intended. The recorder now banks `manual_paused_s` in one `advance_now` choke-point every clock mutator routes through, and feeds the runner `elapsed - manual_paused_s`; a timed step therefore completes while auto-paused (host-test-pinned both ways). **(4) Edges are counters, and banners drop rather than queue.** A `no_std` core carries no event stream, so transitions and end-of-step warnings travel as monotonic sequence numbers in the snapshot's `WorkoutView`; the alert engine fires on advance — `! REP 3/6` (degrading to `! REP 12` when the count outgrows the ten-glyph band, never a truncated count), `! STEP END`, `! WKT DONE` — one rung under the zone ceiling, displacing anything below it (a displaced fuel reminder re-queues per §214), and a zone-blocked edge is **dropped, not owed**, the milestone rule: a stale step banner is worse than none and the page shows the current step regardless. The Workout glance page slots after GuidedRun (the guidance pair closes the live cluster; the page count is 34, pushing `AEFF` beyond the 32-bit `SET1` curation mask alongside `BACK` — both stay uncuratable-but-data-gated per §333), with honest `NOT SYNCED` / `WORKOUT DONE` states and the pace-band vocabulary (`TOO FAST`/`TOO SLOW`) for adherence so the two surfaces cannot disagree. Deliberately deferred: persisting per-step results into the flash blob for the phone's planned-vs-actual review (needs a run-store format bump — the runner keeps results in RAM for the ≥80 % roll-up), and haptic step cues (no motor in the tier-1 BOM). Host-tested throughout; the execution loop, both auto-advance axes, and the banner interleaving are sim-verified over the sim's demo workout under bench_jog; the radio leg is a §314 bench item. This entry replaces the same-day §354 that briefly recorded a parallel implementation of the same feature (display-only, no step-skip, no banner integration) — reverted in this same PR before release; the number is reused so the log stays gapless.

## 355. The Daylight page counts down to the next sun event — the ported solar model fed by the RMC date, gated on the synced timezone

**2026-07-28.** The parity backlog's "Daylight remaining / sunset countdown" row lands at tier 1 — the pull-forward candidate `tier2_scope.md` sized S, the fourth of this batch's items. `watch_core::daylight` ports the seasonal half of web `safety_nudge.ts` (Cooper's declination, solar noon at local 12:00, the −0.833° horizon, polar day/night at the `cos H` clamps) mirrored test-for-test, so nothing is pioneered (§24); what the watch adds is input shaping, the §215 precedent. `Fix` now carries the RMC `ddmmyy` date behind a day-1-31 / month-1-12 plausibility gate in the accumulator (the parser's digit check cannot reject a month 0), `daylight_at` extrapolates the last fix's UTC clock by elapsed uptime the way the idle clock does — fixes are up to a minute apart in Expedition mode, and a frozen countdown reads as a hung watch — and shifts clock **and date** into local civil time (a timezone crosses midnight in both directions, and the declination day must be the runner's day, not Greenwich's). The §293 `SET1` v2 timezone offset becomes the page's data presence (`Recorder::set_tz_offset_min`): a countdown against the wrong midnight is off by whole hours — the difference between "sunset after the aid station" and "sunset before it" — so no offset means no page in the cycle rather than a wrong number on one.

The 35th page (`SUN`, seated between AutoEffort and the still-last BackToStart so the wire-addressable discriminants 0-31 and the safety page's one-tap contract both stand) is a tall-hero glance: the countdown floored to H:MM (the page must never promise light it may not have), SUNRISE/SUNSET on the header row, the event's local clock and the day length below; after sunset the count crosses midnight to tomorrow's sunrise on its own declination day. Two new Settled `Unfed` variants — `MIDNIGHT SUN` / `POLAR NIGHT` — carry the polar seasons, because there the honest answer is the season itself, not a fabricated clock (the model cannot place a rise time inside a polar transition); a missing offset reads `NOT SYNCED`, a dateless fix `AWAITING FIX`. Press costs move within rounding (the §289 BFS model re-derived, still reproducing n=32/33/34 exactly): both grid worsts hold at 6 and 9, the averages go 4.9118 → 5.0286 and 3.8235 → 3.8857, and the linear worst holds 17 — an odd ring has two antipodes. The sim demo settings now push UTC-6 so bench_jog renders the golden pre-dawn case (3:03 to a 04:34 sunrise, 14:53 of day — pinned in `daylight::tests` and re-asserted in the face suite), and `ci_smoke`'s page walk reaches and dumps the page. Host-tested, build-verified on all three feature sets, sim-verified; bench pending with the rest of the board.

## 356. Run-store v4 persists the workout's planned-vs-actual trail, attributed by the WKT1 frame's CRC

**Decided (2026-07-29).** §354's named leftover — the runner kept per-step results in RAM for the ≥80 % roll-up, and a stopped run threw the trail away — closes with a run-store format bump. Four decisions worth recording. **(1) Two record tags, not a sidecar blob.** A settled step's outcome (index, completed/skipped, banked distance/duration/pace) is one more 16-byte cell (tag 2), streamed in close order exactly like laps, so the existing checkpoint ping-pong carries the trail settled before a brown-out for free; a finalize-time summary cell (tag 3) carries the planned step count and the roll-up. Neither tag is ever decimated (the thin keeps every non-point record now), steps cap at the runner's own 64-step bound, and a second summary is refused — it could only contradict the first. **(2) The version bumps even though v3 blobs still decode.** v4 changes nothing about v3's CRC window, so the reader floor stays 3 — but the phone decoder throws on an unknown record tag by design (a CRC-valid cell it cannot name is a bug, not noise), so an un-updated reader must reject a workout-carrying blob *by version* rather than mid-walk. The writer stamps v4 unconditionally; making the version content-dependent (v3 when no workout records) was considered and rejected as a second thing to reason about for zero benefit while both ends live in one repo. **(3) Attribution is the WKT1 frame's CRC, not "whatever the phone pushed last."** The frame carries no id, and results matched to the wrong workout poison the planned-vs-actual review silently. The recorder hashes the armed step list's *canonical* frame at arming (`workout_store::frame_crc`, buffer-free, sharing its byte layout with `encode` through one `step_bytes` helper so the two cannot drift) and the summary carries it; the phone compares against the frame it pushed. The phone-side consequence is fail-closed at the *section* level, not the run level: a trail with no summary (a mid-run-checkpoint recovery — the summary lands only at finalize) or duplicate step indices (a workout re-armed mid-run, splicing two trails) drops the workout section whole and keeps the verified run — the L4 layering applied to a wire format. **(4) The phone stores the trail under its own registered key.** `runFromWatchPayload` forwards the section into `metadata.watch_workout` (owner-only, stripped by `public_runs` in `20270430_001`) rather than the existing `workout_step_results` trio: those entries carry planned identity (kind, targets, tolerance) the watch records don't, and their contract requires a `plan_workout_id` the watch cannot know — the join lands with the product workout-push surface. The transport half of that seam closes in this same batch — `WatchBleTransport.writeWorkout` against the sixth characteristic, `WatchSyncClient.pushWorkout` carrying the wire module's own chunks, and a dev-only Sim Watch push action (a §209 surface, pushing the golden demo workout) — so the CRC handshake is exercisable end-to-end; what remains is the product surface that picks a planned workout and remembers the frame CRC it pushed. The same CRC doubles as the re-push identity on the wrist: `set_workout` ignores a push identical to the armed list, so a BLE retry or a reconnect re-delivering the frame cannot wipe mid-run step progress and manufacture exactly the spliced trail the phone would then discard — re-arming stays what it is for a *different* workout, a deliberate change. Host-tested both sides against shared v4 goldens (the frozen v3 goldens stay as decode-compat vectors), property-tested over the new decoders, and sim-verified: ci_smoke now asserts the smoke stop flushes the armed demo workout's trail before the flash commit.

## 357. BTN5's hold marks a waypoint — the last free gesture, spent on the parity row that had no key

**Decided (2026-07-29).** The parity backlog's "Waypoint marking / save location" row had been blocked on interaction, not maths: the row itself records that "the § 350 grammar has no spare key, so the candidate is a § 351 settings-menu action." That candidate was wrong on inspection. The menu exists **only while idle**, and the position worth saving — a gear cache, a water stash, where the trail was lost — is one the runner is standing on *mid-run*. A menu action would have been an affordance that cannot reach the moment it exists for.

The grammar did have one gesture free after all: **BTN5's hold**. Its tap is the manual lap (and the § 354 workout-step skip), and nothing had ever claimed the tier above it, because the paging keys' hold went to the grid and idle BTN5's went to the menu. So the mark rides the same one-tier, 500 ms boundary the paging keys already train, fires **at** the threshold while the button is still down (§ 350's rule — no release is ever timed blind), and swallows its own release. `lap_press_command(state, Tap)` is test-pinned equal to `command_for(Button::Lap, state)` for every run state: the stop guard and the page grid still read BTN5 through the untiered reducer, and two answers for one press would be two behaviours for one button.

Four choices worth recording. **(1) The mark takes the recorder's distance anchor, not the raw fix stream.** That anchor is the position the run itself is measured from, so the saved point and the recorded track agree about where the runner was; no anchor at all (pre-first-fix, or a run that has only seen rejected fixes) marks nothing rather than a fabricated 0,0, and a press outside a run is refused for the same reason — an idle watch's anchor is the *previous* run's last position. **(2) Marks outlive the run that made them.** Neither `start` nor `reset` clears the store: a stash marked on yesterday's recce is the entire point, so the eight-slot store ages out only by newest-wins eviction (a runner marking a ninth point mid-race cares about the new one, not the stalest). **(3) The page's data-presence bit keys on the STORE, not on a live view** — losing the fix must not pull the page out from under a runner walking back to the stash. **(4) The mark persists on the press, not at stop**, in a `WPT1` record joining `CFG1` and `BND1` on the shared config page: the reason to mark a stash is that you may *not* finish the run that found it. A refused mark writes nothing, so a dead press costs no page erase. That third record is also why `rewrite_config_page` stopped taking one `Option` per record and started taking a `ConfigPage` struct — four positional same-shaped `Option`s is precisely the shape a caller transposes in silence, and the page would still write, just with the bond's bytes where the waypoints go.

The 36th page (`WPT`) sits beside `BACK`, deliberately: the two answer the same "which way, how far" question about different anchors, so they render the same way — hero distance in the same m-then-km shape, the same HDG/BRG sector pair from `trackback` — and cannot read differently. Its empty state needed a new `Unfed` class, `WatchAction`: the datum is one neither the phone nor a sensor nor the run supplies, so the reason line names the gesture (`HOLD BTN5 TO MARK`) — a surface that only says "empty" about a thing a hidden press fills is a surface nobody ever fills. Host-tested; build-verified on all three feature sets; **sim-verified** by the `terrain` scenario (2026-07-29), which is the positive half the first pass could not claim: `$btn5h` drives the hold, the firmware answers `button: Lap -> MarkWaypoint` (the mark tier, not a manual lap) and then `run_flash: persisted waypoints (1)`, and the page enters the BTN4 cycle and renders non-blank. The `pages` scenario's bench_jog walk still asserts the negative — nothing marks a point there, so `WPT` correctly stays out — and the pair is the actual claim: absent when unarmed, present when armed. A data-presence bit wired to the wrong field passes the first test alone.

## 358. The ICE / medical-ID card is an idle FACE, fails the whole card closed, and never enters a log

**Decided (2026-07-29).** The parity backlog's ICE row is worth building precisely because no incumbent makes it a first-class surface: ultras print this on the back of a bib, and the wrist is where a responder looks first. `watch_core::ice` holds five phone-authored lines — holder, blood type, allergies/conditions, emergency contact, number — pushed on `SET1` v6 and mirrored into an `ICE1` flash record.

**Every gate fails the card whole rather than degrading a field.** A clipped allergy line (`PENICILL`) reads as complete and a clipped number dials someone else, so an over-long field is refused at construction, a byte the 1-bit face's ASCII font cannot draw refuses the payload, and so does any byte sitting past a field's NUL terminator — which is exactly what a shorter overwrite of a previous card leaves behind. This makes ICE the **one settings field whose own content can reject the frame**: every other value is merely parsed on the wire and guarded at its setter, but `IceCard` has no setter to guard it, so `decode` is the only place a garbled medical line can be stopped, and a line that reaches a responder is one they will act on. `IceCard` also hand-writes its `defmt::Format` to print presence only — a derived impl would spill a name, blood type, medical history and a next-of-kin number into every logged settings frame, and that log ends up on a cable, in a CI artifact, or in a bug report.

The card is a **third idle face**, not a run page: a responder finds a wrist, not a manual, and a 37-deep run cycle is not somewhere anyone finds anything. BTN4's idle walk grew a third stop (Home → Diagnostics → ICE, one-way, so home is never more than a press away — and the key keeps its § 291 duration-stability, one meaning at any length), and the § 351 menu gained a `MEDICAL ID` action row, because the walk only helps someone who already knows the face is there and the named row is how a runner discovers the card exists and checks it before a race. The layout is label-above-value, never sharing a row: a responder reading a stranger's wrist has no context to expand an abbreviation from, so fields are sized to the face's 21 cells and const asserts pin every label inside it. An empty field reads `--` (nothing recorded) rather than a blank row, which would be indistinguishable from a render that failed; an absent or all-blank card reads `NOT SYNCED`, because five dashes would read as a runner who declined to answer.

`SET1` v6 spends `flags2`'s **last** free bit, which saturates both presence bytes — the next settings field needs a third byte and a version of its own, and two const asserts in `decode` now make that a compile error rather than a frame accepted with a bit nobody defined. The frame grows to 192 bytes, still one write inside the 256-byte ATT MTU, with ~64 bytes of headroom left; `SettingsPush::Applied` correspondingly carries an explicit `large_enum_variant` allow, since the usual remedy is boxing and this crate has no allocator (the value is produced once per closed frame and moved into the queue, so the cost is one short-lived stack frame, not standing memory).

**Known tier-1 limit, recorded rather than papered over:** the card is idle-only, so a responder reaching a watch that is still recording must stop and dismiss the run before BTN4 can walk to it — the wrong order of events for the surface most likely to be read on a collapsed runner. Making it reachable from a run view needs a gesture the § 350 grammar does not have spare (BTN5's hold went to § 357's mark), so it is a tier-2 item. Stated plainly because the whole point of the feature is that it works when the wearer cannot help. Host-tested; build-verified on all three feature sets.

## 359. Climb detection answers two questions — what is underfoot without a course, what is left with one — and never fakes the second

**Decided (2026-07-29).** The parity backlog's "Climb detection / ClimbPro-style ascent view" row is the one item in this batch with **no web helper to port**: the app has per-leg vert in `roadbook`, but live segmentation is new firmware work. `watch_core::climb` splits it in two, because a runner on a hill asks two different questions and only one of them is always answerable. `ClimbDetector` segments the climb they are **in** from the recorder's own distance + altitude stream and needs no course; `crest_ahead` answers how much is **left** from the pushed course profile — the headline Garmin number — and exists exactly when a course does. The live half never fabricates the second answer when it has no course: the watch cannot see the hill, and a "remaining" of `--` would read as a crest at zero metres.

**Both edges are hysteretic and deliberately blunt.** A climb opens only past 20 m of gain above the last low point at ≥ 2 % average grade, and closes only once 10 m has been lost below the climb's high point. Without both, barometric noise and the dips every real climb carries would open and close a "climb" every few hundred metres — and a page that re-zeroes on every roller is worse than no page: a runner pacing a 400 m ascent would watch their banked gain reset three times on the way up. The drop threshold is what makes the high point the **crest** rather than the last sample, and the same rule runs the profile search, so a shelf in a staircase climb is not reported as the top — which would tell a runner they were nearly done halfway up. The close threshold is deliberately smaller than the opening one: a false close costs the runner their banked gain, a late close only holds a finished climb on screen a few hundred metres longer. Grades come from a climb's own endpoints, never from the last two samples — a 1 m baro twitch across a 5 m step reads as a 20 % grade, and the number on the page has to be the hill, not the sensor.

Two integration choices. **The detector rides the same altitude sample `feed_gap` already takes**, alongside the live-GAP grade and the elevation sparkline, so a hill cannot register on one page and not another; `start` resets it, because a run beginning at a lower trailhead than the last one ended would otherwise open a phantom ascent on its first fix. **The crest half needed no new wire at all**: the distance-even profile the RouteElev page already carries (§ 334's `CRS1` v2 series, resampled by `course_profile`) is exactly the series to search, and the nav task's along-course position is already fed for the cut-off ETA — so the crest is derived per snapshot rather than banked, and shrinks with every fix instead of at sync time. It is measured from the runner rather than from their grid sample, which on a 100 km course is worth a kilometre.

The 37th page (`CLMB`) **heads** the course cluster rather than sitting beside the run's own elevation profile: on a mountain course it is the question asked most, the first thing checked when the trail tilts up. It leads with what is left when a course names a crest and falls back to what has been banked when it does not, with the label row saying which — the same number measured from two places is only useful if the runner knows where from. Flat ground with nothing ahead is a new **Settled** `Unfed` (`NO CLIMB`), not `NOT SYNCED`: a working page must not send a runner looking for a phone.

Pages 36 and 37 are the **first to move a grid worst since the § 289 model was built** (the BFS re-derived, still reproducing n=32 exactly): the symmetric worst goes 6 → 7 at page 36 and the forward-only 9 → 10 at page 37, the averages 3.8857 → 4.0541 and 5.0286 → 5.2432, and the linear worst 17 → 18 at page 36. Five `{±1, ±4}` moves cover 37 distinct offsets (everything within ±20 bar the gaps the ±4 stride leaves near the edges), and a 36-page ring is the first whose furthest cell falls outside them — so the cursor needs a sixth move and the page costs `1 + 6` = 7. Recorded plainly rather than rounded away: the everyday cost is unchanged (a filtered mask is ~12 pages, worst 4), but the full-mask ceiling has stopped being flat. The next thresholds are computed too: the forward-only worst goes 10 → 11 at page 42, the symmetric 7 → 8 at page 44. Host-tested; build-verified on all three feature sets; **sim-verified** by the `terrain` scenario (2026-07-29), which supplies the terrain the flat fixture cannot: on `mountain_loop` with the BMP581 model's triangle profile running, the baro's cumulative gain clears the 20 m a climb opens at and `CLMB` enters the BTN4 cycle and renders non-blank. Arming that profile is load-bearing rather than scene-setting — `feed_gap` takes `baro_alt_m.or(fix.alt_m)`, baro FIRST, so the fixture's own GGA altitude ramp is shadowed by the model's static default and the detector would see level ground however steep the fixture is. The bench_jog walk still asserts the negative, and the pair is the claim.

## 360. The sim's panel dumps became viewable, and the first thing they showed was a bar painted over a text row

**Decided (2026-07-29).** The Renode sim has dumped panel frames since § 208, but only ever to assert one thing: the frame is **not blank**. Nothing made a dump *viewable*, so the only way to look at the firmware's UI was `bin/watch-sim.sh --gui` and paging through thirty-odd screens by hand — which means every layout problem this project has ever had was found by a human happening to notice one. `bin/watch-shots.sh` closes that: two boots (a full BTN4 lap mid-run on `mountain_loop` with § 359's climb and § 357's waypoint armed, so the terrain pages are in the cycle; then `--no-autostart` for the three idle faces and the § 351 menu), one PNG per screen at the panel's true 168x144, and a self-contained contact sheet. 25 screens on the first honest run.

**What it caught immediately.** #609's race-phase line went onto the pacer page's row 3 while the ahead/behind centre bar already owned that row full-width, and the bar had been painting through the phase text on the glass ever since.
