Nothing failed, because nothing *could*: `face.rs` tests assert row strings, `widgets.rs` tests assert bar columns, and **no test composed the two layers** — the placement contract was a comment in a module header, enforced by nobody. `overlay_never_paints_over_face_text` now draws text and overlay into separate framebuffers and sweeps every page whose bar shares the panel with text, at the widest values the face can write, asserting no overlay inks a cell a glyph occupies. Cell granularity, not pixel: an in-row bar legitimately shares a *row* (the workout and zone bars do), but a bar and a glyph in one 8x16 cell is corruption whether or not their ink happens to interleave.

The fix moves the bar, not the text, and the page is why: it carries nine rows of content in nine rows, so there is no blank row to move to. The bar goes **in-row on row 7, past the widest `DIST` value** — off the row it was designed for (directly under the hero whose signed time it encodes) and onto the row whose value agrees with it in sign, which is what a centre-out bar communicates. Recorded as the compromise it is: the gauge is now further from its hero than the original design intended, and the alternative was deleting one of the three encodings of `ahead_s` the page already carries.

**Two harness lessons, both about trusting a dump.** `ci_smoke`'s `wait_for_no_alert` cannot be used for a long walk — past roughly 100 s the sim's shortened cadences go banner-to-banner and `record: alert cleared` stops arriving, which aborted the first walk eight pages early. And the composer logs its page line **before** it draws and flushes, so a dump sent the instant that line decodes can read the panel's *previous* frame. That one is not hypothetical: it is how this harness first "proved" the two idle faces render identically, which read exactly like an `IDLE_VIEW` that never reached the composer. Both rejections are now measured **on the captured pixels** — a banner is a solid inverse-video band over the hero rows, a stale frame is byte-identical to the previous screen — because the artifact is the thing being judged and a log line is an inference about it. A screen that stays bannered or stale after four tries is still captured and says so in its caption; a hole in the sheet would be worse.

The idle faces also gained the line they never had. The button task has always logged which face a press *selected*; `ui: idle <View>` is the separate claim that the composer *followed it onto the panel* — the same two-claim cross-check § 208's page walk makes every press, and the pair disagreeing is its own bug class. Change-gated like the page line, so a task designed to sleep between events gains no standing per-second reason to emit.

**The window itself.** The `--gui` canvas showed the panel as pure `#fff` on `#000` between two flat grey strips with five boxes reading `BTN1`..`BTN5` — a wiring diagram you had to already know the § 350 grammar to drive. It now paints the panel in the reflective silver-green a Sharp MIP actually reads as (there is no backlight; its white was never `#fff`), gives the case a lit top edge, a shadowed bottom, a rim around the recessed glass and rounded corners, and labels each key with what it *does*. Geometry is deliberately untouched — `CanvasWidth`, `ButtonX`, `ButtonY` all hold — so the analyzer's click mapping and the `HitButton` boxes are the same pixels they were, and this is purely how those pixels are coloured. `DumpFrame` keeps its own flat black/white pair rather than the canvas palette, because its bytes are what every assertion reads; `DumpCanvas` is the new sibling for the shell, which has no truth to assert and until now could not be reviewed without a display attached.

**What a screenshot does NOT prove**, on the same terms as § 314: nothing here reads a glyph. A capture says the named screen composed and inked pixels — page identity comes from the ui task's own line, and layout and value correctness remain host-test claims (`render/src/preview.rs`, `core/`). It is *sim-verified* evidence and no more; see `docs/custom_watch/quality_standards.md`. And the sheet is not the whole UI: thirteen pages have no `SET1` wire field to arm them at all, so a 25-screen sheet is the ceiling of what the sim can currently show, not of what the watch renders.

## 361. The run view spends its cells on values — a glyph for the GPS row, the unit beside its hero, and the hero band every page reserved and thirteen never used

**Decided (2026-07-29).** § 360 made the panel viewable, and the first sheet showed three things no host test could have failed on, because none of them is a wrong value — all three are cells spent saying what the panel had already said, on a 21x9 grid where a cell is 0.5% of everything the watch can tell a runner. Measured before deciding, because the first eyeball impression ("the pages are half empty") was wrong: mean **ink rows were 6.6 of 9** across the 37-page cycle, so most pages were dense and the waste was concentrated, not general.

**`GPS` was a word on twenty-one pages.** Every run page ends on the same GPS glance, and every one but the dashboard spelled the label out — five of twenty-one cells, on a row whose meaning is fixed across the whole cycle. The dashboard had used `Icon::Satellite` in that gutter since the icon table existed, and the glyph says strictly more than the word: its `SatSearch0`/`SatSearch1`/`Satellite` frames also convey *acquiring*, which the word needs a second field (`ACQUIRING`) to say. `page_icons` now labels `GPS_ROW` on the whole cycle. The cheap version would have been a per-page icon list; instead `write_gps_row` lost the `label` parameter altogether, so the icon and the cleared gutter cannot disagree — there is no longer a way to express the disagreement.

**Units had drifted a row away from the numbers they measure.** A `0.08` hero over a `DISTANCE  KM` label row reads as a heading and a number, not as a measurement; on the pace page the unit sat under a different word again. They got there for a real reason: the generated numeral faces spell digits, `.`, `:`, `-` and `+` and nothing else, so one letter in the hero string demotes the whole value to the pixel-doubled 8x16 text font. The Workout page's distance hero was paying exactly that — `9.60 KM` in doubled strokes. So the unit becomes its **own channel**: `face::page_hero_unit` decides it, `ui_frame::hero_unit_cell` places it at 1x on the hero's own baseline (row 2 under the 32x48 face, row 1 under the 16x32), and the number keeps the numeral face. Which is where every watch a runner has worn puts it.

Three couplings fall out, and each is handled rather than left latent. The unit joins the tall face's **width budget**, so a 1000 km hero steps down a size rather than go unlabelled — the same "smaller and complete beats larger and truncated" rule the fit test already encoded. It lands on `RUN_MARKER_ROW` under the two-row faces, so `hero_row_cells` counts it and the standing battery / fuel marker still refuses rather than gets half-eaten. And it is suppressed on a placeholder, because `-- KM` puts a unit on a number that is not there — gated by **one** rule (`hero_has_value`: the hero holds a digit) rather than each of 37 arms re-deriving its own fed check.

**Thirteen pages reserved the hero band and left it blank.** `body_top_row` is the contract for which rows a page's own text may write, and the phone-pushed summary pages all reserve two — then stated their headline in an 8x16 row indistinguishable from the rows contextualising it. Recap said `1500 KM` in the same type as the streak beside it. A fifth of the panel, at the top, on a third of the cycle. Each now headlines the number the page is *about*, and the row that used to carry it is **dropped** rather than kept as a small copy of the big one. Mean ink rows: 6.6 → **7.3**.

Two of those heroes are shaped by the number rather than the layout. Race day is **unsigned**, with `TO GO` / `TODAY` / `AGO` below, because a minus sign in front of a countdown reads as a negative number of days rather than as a date already past. And PR age inside a week writes no bucket row at all: a small `5 DAYS` under a big `5 DAYS` is not a second fact. `every_page_that_reserves_a_hero_band_fills_it` pins the contract from the side it had never been pinned from, and structurally — `Page::Nav` is exempt because its `body_top_row` is 0, so it reserves nothing to waste, not because it is on an exemption list.

**One real bug fell out of the third change.** The state tag's rule is refuse-rather-than-truncate: a half-written `RE` is not a degraded `REC`, it is a tag naming a different state. But `write_tag` sees only row text, and the hero is drawn *after* the rows, over exactly its own span — so a hero wide enough to reach the tag clipped it. Live on the dashboard past 100 hours, where the elapsed hero is nine medium glyphs, eighteen of twenty-one cells: three left for `REC`, one too few for `AUTO`, which rendered as `UTO` on precisely the multi-day runs where knowing the recorder auto-paused matters most. `apply_hero_clearance` is the same refusal from the hero's side, and reads the band's extent from `hero_band_rows` so it cannot disagree with what is drawn.

**And one redundancy the third change created, removed in the same pass.** `write_unfed` had put `--` beside the page's label, which was right while the band above it might be empty. It no longer can be, so an unsynced page read `FITNESS --` under a 16x32 `--` over `NOT SYNCED` — one absence, three times, in four of nine rows. The label drops its dashes; the hero keeps them, which is where a runner at arm's length reads them. A per-*row* placeholder is a different claim and keeps its own: `HDG  --` says one field is missing while the rest of the page is fed.

**A fourth kind of duplicate, found by writing the guard for the third.** Three pages already carried an exact small copy of their headline before any of this — `WEAR 87 %` under an `87%` hero, `CARB 0 G` under a `0`-carbs hero, `DIST 0.08 KM` under a `0.08 KM` hero — and thirteen more would have started the moment they gained heroes. All three rows go: GearWear keeps its verdict word and its bar (a graphical restatement is not a textual one), Fuel says the fluid to carry instead, DistanceBand keeps the band and its window. `no_page_restates_its_hero_in_a_body_row` matches a body row holding the hero's digits *and* the hero's unit, deliberately narrow on both counts — a row may legitimately carry the same **number** as a different quantity (the Climb page's `OVER 83 M` is ground covered under an ascent hero), and a member of an ordered ladder stays even when it duplicates, because dropping `EASY` from the five training paces leaves four rungs and an inference. TrainingPaces is therefore a *named* exemption rather than a silent one. The same sweep is what caught the Zones page still labelling its row `HR  BPM` under a hero whose unit is now `BPM`.

**And three defects in the fixture, all one shape.** Writing that guard surfaced `fed_snapshot` giving independent fields a single value: average, current and grade-adjusted pace were all `99:59`, the crest-ahead and climb-underfoot gains were both `99999`, and the current and best streaks were both `9999` — so the guard read three legitimate rows as restatements. Each is distinct now at the same cell width, so the width stress the fixture exists for is unchanged. The quieter problem it also closes is worth naming: while two independent fields hold one number, a test asserting either of them passes reading the other.

**The satellite glyph was redrawn twice**, because the first change took it from one page to thirty-seven. It was the lightest icon in the table (36 ink pixels against 54–110 for its siblings) and off-centre, spanning cols 1–10 of sixteen where the others span 2–13 — tolerable on one row of one page, not as the label on every run page.

The first redraw drew three arcs *from* the shared anchor dot, and looking at the rendered cell is what showed why that fails: arcs that all begin at one point overlap near it and separate only at their far tips, so at sixteen pixels the three collapsed into a single diagonal wedge that read as a hook. Every check the table had passed on it — the frames were distinct, the ink grew 19 → 37 → 59 — because ink totals cannot see a merge. The arcs are now **concentric about** the dot rather than radiating from it, and vertically symmetric so their apexes rasterise as flat runs instead of stair-steps: 26 → 52 → **84** ink across the acquiring frames, each arc a band with clear panel between it and its neighbours.

`each_search_frame_shows_its_arcs_as_separate_bands` is what makes that a claim rather than an intention. The fan is concentric, so the cell's centre line is a ray outward from the dot and must cross exactly one ink band per arc plus the dot itself — two, three, four across the three frames. It fails on the merged version at frame 0. Growing ink was never the property worth pinning; *drawn apart* is, and it is the one a runner reads.

**The same look at the panel found the bang rendering as a colon.** Every alert banner is `!` plus a word, and the `!` in the 8x16 table had kept its top serif and its dot and lost the stem between them — two short marks, a colon with the upper dot raised a row. So the banner a runner sees when the watch says drink, eat, ease off, or *you are at a cut-off* opened `: DRINK`, with the mark that separates an alert from a label reading as punctuation. It is the same lost-hairline failure `gen_font.py`'s repair pass exists for (§ 4704's `+` packing byte-identical to `-`, and `|` shipping blank), one step short of the collision that would have caught it: `!` and `:` differ as bytes, so nothing looked.

The trigger widens rather than the threshold. A glyph-wide heuristic was measured first — "a stroke the supersampled pass renders at more than twice the 1x length" — and rejected at 33 of 95 glyphs flagged, because the 2x pass puts most stems across two columns where 1x picks one, so it reads sub-pixel placement as damage. `DAMAGED_GLYPHS` names the characters whose damage stops short of a collision instead, repaired outright through the existing supersampler; the regenerated table is byte-identical everywhere but `!`. `bang_is_a_stem_over_a_dot_not_a_second_colon` holds the shape from the driver side — a taller unbroken run than the colon's, and exactly two ink-to-blank transitions so the dot cannot fuse into a `|` — which is what keeps the named list from quietly falling behind the font.

**What none of this changes.** No value moved, no page left or joined the cycle, and no button means anything new — so § 350's press grammar, § 284's curation mask and § 286's order all stand untouched. The evidence rung is unchanged too: the sheet that motivated the work is *sim-verified* (§ 360, § 314), and layout correctness remains a host-test claim — `every_run_page_labels_its_gps_row_with_the_satellite`, `every_hero_unit_has_a_hero_to_label_and_room_beside_it`, and the band guard above are where these three decisions are actually enforced.

**A coverage hole found on the way in, worth recording separately.** `fed_snapshot()` backs every page-wide guard in `face.rs` — the grid-fit sweep, the hero-band placement guard, the state-tag sweep — and it only ever filled the *phone-pushed* views. Pacer, Workout, CutoffEta, Climb, Waypoint and RacePredictor derive from live sensor state, so six page bodies had never been walked in any of them, only in their empty state. All three sweeps pass unchanged with them fed: nothing was broken behind the hole, it was simply unwatched. That it went unnoticed until a density measurement needed a realistic snapshot is the argument for measuring rather than eyeballing, twice over.

## 362. The sim harness asserts the rails it had only ever run — and the fixture loop that hid a bug from the guard written for it

**Date:** 2026-07-30

Four Renode scenarios were green, and three things that had never been asserted at all were still green underneath them.

**The optical-HR rail and the phone link had no assertion anywhere.** `sim/Max86177.cs` was built on 2026-07-19 specifically to take the optical-HR path off the bench gate, and no scenario since had read a BPM off it — the TWIM EasyDMA master, the tagged MEAS1/MEAS2 stream, the AGC and the pulse detector could all break with every scenario still passing. The phone link is worse, because it is a whole rail: `watch.resc` bridges UARTE1 to a TCP socket, the mobile dev screen consumes it, and nothing had ever opened that socket. The panel could be perfect while the link emitted nothing, and the only way to find out was for a human to run the mobile screen. Both are now folded into `smoke` rather than given scenarios of their own — neither needs anything that boot was not already doing, and a scenario costs a whole emulator. The link assertion cross-checks the fix against the one the decoded log reported, so the claim is that one parsed fix reached *both* rails, not that each produced something.

**`gps_dropout` was the fixture that found a real bug and the only one with no scenario.** It was written for the 2026-07-19 manual pass and caught the un-ported `run_recorder` #330 gap re-anchor — distance frozen for the rest of a run after any 1 Hz dropout that displaced the runner past `MAX_JUMP_M`. Fixed the same day, guarded since by two host tests over `Recorder`, and by nothing at all end to end: the fixture stayed a manual poke, so the NMEA → parser → publish-cadence → recorder path that surfaced the bug had no regression guard. `dropout` is that guard.

**Writing it is what found the harness defect worth recording.** The first version passed against a firmware with the re-anchor branch deliberately disabled. `bin/watch-sim.sh` loops the NMEA file, and the loop teleports the runner ~354 m back to the fixture's start — from where they walk *toward* the anchor the broken recorder is still holding, until the delta falls back under `MAX_JUMP_M` over a dt of minutes and is accepted, crediting ~98 m in one lump. Distance resumes, late and for entirely the wrong reason, and a resume assertion reads it as the re-anchor working. Measured at t=220.7 s against a void ending at t=126.9 s.

Two fixes were tried before the one that shipped, and both are worth recording because they are the obvious ones. **A time window** — require the resume within N virtual seconds of the void — is the wrong tool: Renode's virtual clock runs at a ratio to wall time that swings with host load (between ~1x and ~2x on one machine in one afternoon), so the wall-clock loop's distance from the void is not a fixed number of virtual seconds to sit inside of. It survives as a secondary promptness claim only. **Stopping the feed after one pass** (`--nmea-once`) is worse: however the feed is stopped, the firmware stops receiving sentences that were written before it stopped, so the fixture silently loses its tail — gps_dropout delivered its clean opening leg and then nothing at all, and the void never ended. Holding the writing fd open past the last line did not change it, so the flag was removed rather than shipped broken; whatever buffers between the feeder and the emulated UARTE only drains while the writer is still writing.

What shipped instead asserts on the run's own evidence: `fixture_restart_at` finds the restart in the published-fix stream — a step between consecutive fixes past 200 m, which separates the ~354 m teleport from both the ~3 m ordinary step and the 122 m the runner covered during the void — and the resume search refuses to read past it. No clock is involved, so nothing about it moves when the host speeds up or slows down.

The scenario is verified to **fail** as well as pass — with the re-anchor disabled the void and freeze assertions still pass and the resume one reports the frozen plateau by name. A guard that has never been seen to fail is not known to be a guard, and this one had already proved that about itself.

**And the phone link now opens on the present.** Renode's server-socket provider queues everything the UART wrote while no client was attached, and `CreateServerSocketTerminal` defaults `flushOnConnect` to False — so a client attaching ten minutes into a run received the frame from `uptime_s = 1` and every one since before it caught up. That is the wrong default for this consumer: the mobile app's Sim watch link screen and a bare `ncat` are both LIVE views, and a live view whose first values are ten minutes stale is worse than one that starts empty. `watch.resc` passes the fourth argument. The assertion added above is what keeps it — the first frame off a fresh connection has to carry an `uptime_s` within 20 s of the run's own clock at the moment the socket was opened, which a replay of the boot cannot — and it is the reason that assertion compares the NEWEST fix on each rail rather than the first: the frames are live now, so the pair that can agree is the pair sampled at about the same moment.

**The sim's alert cadences moved behind their own feature.** `sim-alerts` carries the shortened fuel / distance / time / pace arms that `bin/watch-shots.sh` had no way to ask a sim to go without. They exist for the `alerts` scenario and are noise to everything else — past ~100 s they overlap into a continuous banner, and a banner is a solid band over the two hero rows of whatever page is on screen. That cost six of twenty-one run screens on the first contact sheet, `page-Dashboard` and `page-Climb` among them, the latter's entire hero replaced by `! DRINK`. Dropping `sim-autostart` would have silenced them too and would have taken with it the demo settings that arm most of the pages worth photographing, which is the whole reason the split is a separate feature rather than a wider switch.

**What none of this changes.** No firmware behaviour moved: `sim-alerts` gates arming that was already sim-only, and every default and hardware path is byte-for-byte what it was. The rungs are unchanged too — the new assertions earn *sim-verified* for exactly the observables they name (§ 314), the link one says nothing about BLE, which can never be sim-verified, and `dropout` reports a host too slow to run the fixture as exactly that rather than as a frozen recorder.

## 363. The run view's headline metrics are a named catalogue, not thirty-six arms of a page match

**Date:** 2026-07-30

The custom watch has 37 fixed single-purpose glance pages and exactly one multi-field screen (the Dashboard). Against Garmin — where a runner composes their own screens from a field catalogue — that reads as a missing feature, and the obvious response is to build composable screens: a metric catalogue, a `SCR1` wire frame, a flash record, a phone-side editor.

**We built only the catalogue, and deliberately stopped there.**

**The gap was mis-stated.** "Garmin lets you compose screens" describes Garmin's *solution*, not our problem. Configurability exists because Garmin ships to millions of runners with irreconcilable preferences and cannot curate for each; Coros ships fewer, simpler, curated screens and is praised for it. This watch has one user — the owner — and § 71 defers watch development indefinitely with an amendment permitting owner-personal tier-1 work only. For one user, curation is the same outcome without a byte format, a flash record, an editor, seven ARB locales and two byte-identical iOS twins. The accurate gap is narrower and cheaper: *there is one multi-field screen and no way to have a second one tuned differently.*

**The durable artifact is the abstraction, not the feature.** `face::page_hero` and `face::page_hero_unit` already reduced all 37 pages to `(value, unit)` — they were a metric formatter keyed on the wrong thing. `Metric` (34 variants) plus `hero_metric(page)` re-keys them, and the two public entry points survive as thin wrappers, so no caller moved. The whole change is a refactor of the render layer: no wire, no flash, no product surface. It needed no tier override and no § 209 argument because it is neither the T3 roadmap row nor an authoring surface — **it dissolves those questions rather than winning them.**

**Three pages share one metric, and now say so.** Distance, Splits and DistanceBand all headline distance covered and differ only in the body beneath. As three arms of one `match page` they were three copies free to diverge — one rounding change to a single arm and two of the three would have disagreed about the same number, on the same run, one press apart. `pages_sharing_a_metric_render_the_same_hero` is the assertion the old shape could not make.

**What we deliberately did not build, and why deferring costs nothing.** `SCR1`, a seventh GATT characteristic, a config-page record, and a field picker are all *additive* on top of a catalogue that now exists; nothing here gets rewritten when they land. And each is downstream of a question we cannot answer yet:

- **The unfed problem is unsolved.** `unfed` classifies empty states by what the runner can *do* — "sync your phone" vs "run further" vs "there is genuinely no climb". A full-page empty state has room for a reason line; a slot does not, and a bare `--` collapses all three into one shrug. Freezing a byte layout around that is how a version bump is earned.
- **The right layout is a bench question.** Measured at 45 cm: the big numeral subtends 38.8 arcmin, the medium 19.4. Two stacked fields keep both values in the top tier and need no new primitive; a 2×2 needs a cell-aligned column offset on `draw_bignum_med_hero` and still cannot fit `1:23:45` in an 80 px slot. Which a tired runner actually reads is a step-4 claim by our own `quality_standards.md`, and the simulator cannot settle it.
- **The press-cost ceiling is real.** The § 289 model is a function of page count alone: N ≤ 6 custom screens preserves both published ceilings (7 full-mask, 4 everyday); N = 7 costs the first, N = 8 costs both.

**And the priority argument, which outranks all of it.** § 82 makes tier-1 done when one real outdoor run syncs end-to-end from the bench prototype. No parts exist; nothing in this firmware has executed on silicon. Every rung above *sim-verified* is unearned for the entire codebase. Adding a configurability system to a watch that has never recorded a real step optimises a surface nobody has touched — the 37 pages we have are themselves unproven, and making them configurable would not prove them.

**The trigger that reverses this.** If the watch is intended for anyone but the owner, configurability moves from premature to necessary and the design is ready — the five-way investigation behind this entry sized the whole vertical (frame at 51 bytes for 8×4, single ATT write; config-page record at offset 384 with 3,736 bytes free; contiguous seating at discriminants 1..N). § 209 already names the condition in its own words: pairing and sync UX pioneer on web "when the watch becomes a product track". Until that fires, the catalogue is the part worth having.

**Rendering-neutral, and pinned as such.** The host suite went 2151 → 2154 with the three new guards and no existing test changed; `smoke`, `pages` and `terrain` stay green under Renode. That the *existing* suite passed untouched is the evidence that no pixel moved.

## 364. A composed screen's empty slot names what the runner can do, and the three rails under it are built

**Date:** 2026-07-30

[§ 363](#363-the-run-views-headline-metrics-are-a-named-catalogue-not-thirty-six-arms-of-a-page-match) built the metric catalogue and stopped, listing three things it would not build and one question it could not answer. This entry closes the question and builds the rails; the one piece still owed is named at the bottom rather than left implicit.

**The unfed problem, resolved: a slot shows its class, not its reason.** `unfed` classifies an empty state by what the runner can *do* about it, and spends a whole reason line plus a hint line saying so. A slot on a composed screen has neither — it is one value and a five-cell label, two or three to a screen. So the question was never *which reason* survives but *how much of one*, and the answer is `UnfedClass`, because that enum is already cut along the only axis a runner acts on. Five words carry what fourteen `Unfed` variants say: **SYNC** (act on the phone), **WAIT** (a sensor has not produced a first reading), **RUN** (the run has not met the gate), **NONE** (fed, and the honest answer is none), **MARK** (the runner fills this one with a button).

§ 363 called a bare `--` the alternative and was right that it collapses "your phone never sent this", "keep running", and "there is genuinely no climb here" into one shrug. What makes that unacceptable rather than merely terse is the surface: the collapse happens on the *only* surface with no body text to disambiguate it. A runner who cannot separate a broken sync from a settled answer either chases a fault that is not there or ignores one that is — and on a watch whose argument is what a tired runner reads at hour 60, that is the failure mode that matters. The tokens are words, so they draw in the text face rather than a numeral one: a slot showing a word is visibly not a slot showing a measurement, before it is read. `DONE` on a finished workout step set that precedent.

**The cost of the answer is a second match, and a guard rather than a promise.** `metric_unfed` mirrors `metric_hero` over the same 34 variants, so the real risk is not the vocabulary but the two drifting. `a_metric_is_unfed_exactly_when_its_hero_is_a_placeholder` walks the catalogue fed and unfed, with and without a pulse, and fails if a metric claims a reason while rendering a number or renders `--` while claiming to be fed. It was verified by mutation, not by inspection. `is_unfed_hero` is what it asks with, deliberately **not** `ui_frame::hero_has_value`: that one answers on digits alone, which is right for deciding whether to place a unit and wrong here, because `DONE` carries no digit and is still a value.

`Unfed` gains `AwaitingPulse`. No page ever needed it — the zones page draws `HR --` inside an otherwise-fed body — but a slot that *is* the pulse has no body to be fed, so it needed a reason of its own instead of borrowing a wrong one.

**The layout question § 363 sent to the bench was already answered by the frame.** `SCREEN_SLOTS` is 3: `Duo` keeps both values in the 32x48 hero and needs no new drawing primitive, `Trio` spends one on a hero and drops two to the 16x32 face, and the 2×2 that § 363 costed at a cell-aligned column offset is layout byte 3 — a reserved seat `decode` refuses until something can draw it. The bench claim that remains is which a tired runner prefers, not which we can build.

**Radio, flash and phone are built; the wire is pinned across both languages.** The push is one more write characteristic, **unchunked** — the whole set is 28 bytes, so it fits a single ATT write and an offset-ordered assembler like `course` and `workout` carry would buy nothing but a reset-recovery contract to get wrong. Flash takes the config page at offset 512, past the ICE card, carried forward by the same read-everything / erase / write-everything rewrite the bond, waypoint and ICE records already ride; the const-assert chain now runs base → bond → waypoints → ICE → screens → page end, so an offset growing into its neighbour is a compile error. The `record` task closes the loop — read at boot, publish, and persist a push only when it differs from what flash holds, which is also what stops its own boot publication costing an erase. The set is a latest-value `Watch` like `WORKOUT` rather than a queue like `SETTINGS`, because one frame is the complete answer and a coalesced intermediate is not a lost edit.

Fail-closed is whole-frame throughout, `ice`'s rule rather than `CFG1`'s: a screen whose third slot silently blanked would read as a complete screen the runner authored, and there is nothing on the wrist to say otherwise. Refusing the set leaves the 37 built-in pages working, which is the L4 answer.

`watch_screens.dart` mirrors the encoder, and the golden frame is what proves the two agree — the Dart test asserts the same hex string the Rust one does, so a reorder of either enum fails there rather than silently re-pointing every screen already pushed to a watch.

**The cycle and the layout, built.** The four `Screen` pages seat immediately **after** the Dashboard. A screen a runner composed is by construction the thing they most want to glance at, so burying it behind thirty-six built-ins would defeat the feature; inserting at the front rather than the back is what keeps `BackToStart` last, one long-press from home, which is the one ordering property the safety page cannot lose. That renumbers every page bit — sanctioned on the same grounds § 350's renumber was, zero deployed watches — and costs nothing downstream, because `profiles.rs` builds its masks from `Page::bit` symbolically and `statusbar`'s rank math needs only declaration order to equal cycle order, which it still does. The pages are gated on the runner having actually composed them, so an unpushed watch walks exactly the 37 built-ins with no blank seats; the recorder holds the *count* and nothing else, so there is one copy of the screens and it cannot disagree with itself about how many there are.

**Slot 0 is a tall hero at row 0 — exactly what a glance page's is.** So it feeds the existing hero and inherits the band decision, the unit placement and the run-marker clearance untouched, and only the slots beneath it are new drawing. That is the whole reason the layouts were cut this way. A `Duo` is two 32x48 values at rows 0-2 and 4-6 with a label under each; a `Trio` is that hero over two 16x32 values whose labels sit to their right on their own baselines; the GPS row survives on all three, because a composed screen does not get to hide the fix quality.

**The simulator caught what the geometry tests could not.** A placement's band is a *nominal* request. The numeral faces carry digits, `.`, `:`, `-` and `+`, and the primitive **skips glyphs it has no index for** — so a word does not render badly, it renders as *nothing*, and the row is simply blank. Every unfed slot holds a word (the class tokens above) and a settled workout step holds `DONE`, which makes that the common case rather than the edge one; the first sim run of a `Duo` drew two labels and no values at all. `ui_frame::slot_band` falls back to the doubled text face — the same call `hero_band` already makes for a page's own hero — and `every_value_a_slot_can_hold_lands_in_a_face_that_can_draw_it` walks every token on every layout in every slot plus the whole catalogue fed and unfed, reproducing the blank panel when the fallback is removed. **This is the argument for the sim rung**: four host guards asserted the arithmetic was right and every one of them passed while the panel was empty.

**Sim-verified** ([§ 314](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md)). A `screens` scenario boots three seeded screens through `state::SCREENS` — the same channel a phone push feeds, so the real publish → gate → render path runs rather than a shortcut into the face — and asserts they are the first three pages after the Dashboard, that each draws a non-blank and *distinct* panel, and that the fourth, uncomposed, is **not** in the cycle. It boots `--no-alerts` because the shortened sim fuel cadences overlap into a continuous banner and a banner owns the hero band, which would have made the slot-0 assertions vacuous. `pages` and `terrain` re-run green, so the renumber moved no built-in walk; `sim-screens` is opt-in for that same reason.

**What is still not proven, and cannot be here.** That a tired runner actually reads a `Duo` or a `Trio` at 45 cm. The arcmin arithmetic behind the layouts (38.8 for the big face, 19.4 for the medium) is derivation, not measurement, and § 92's step-4 rung is a bench claim by our own standards. The panel renders them; whether they are *legible* at hour 60 by headlamp is on the tier-1 bench checklist, not in this entry.

**The § 82 priority argument still stands and is unchanged by any of this.** Nothing in this firmware has executed on silicon. These rails are built because they are additive and now cheap, not because the 37 pages beneath them have been proven.

## 365. Owner override: build BLE external-sensor pairing now — the one tier-2 item that needs no new silicon

**Date:** 2026-07-30

**What was authorised, and by whom.** The repository owner authorised building **BLE external-sensor pairing** — a GATT central role that pairs the watch with a standard heart-rate chest strap and feeds its readings into the existing HR pipeline — on 2026-07-30, overriding the [§ 71](#71-own-hardware-an-ultra-marathon-watch-stays-research-only-watch-development-is-deferred-indefinitely) tier-2 gate. `docs/custom_watch/roadmap.md` carries "BLE sensor pairing" as an explicit **T2** row, and none of § 71's three triggers (a paying user base large enough to fund a parallel hardware effort, an ODM approach, a hardware co-founder) has fired. The precedent for recording an override this way is [§ 211](#211-owner-override-build-the-full-watchphonesupabase-run-sync-vertical-now-despite-the-tier-2-gate), where the same owner overrode the same gate to build the finished-run sync vertical. As there, **a future reader must not treat the presence of this code as evidence the § 71 triggers flipped.**

**Why this item and not another.** `docs/custom_watch/tier2_scope.md` puts the Apollo510B silicon migration at P1 — an XL blocker with no Embassy HAL, which almost every other tier-2 item sits behind. Strap pairing is the one that does not: it runs on the nRF52840 the bench prototype already targets, through the `nrf-softdevice` stack [§ 210](#210-tier-1-ble-s140-softdevice-is-a-compile-verified-feature-gated-build--mutually-exclusive-with-the-sim-off-by-default) already pinned, and needs no new part, no PCB, and no phone/backend change. It is also the item that most directly serves § 82's Definition of Done: a chest strap is how a bench prototype gets a *trustworthy* HR trace on the one outdoor run that completes tier 1, without waiting on the optical AFE's uncalibrated AGC and unmeasured motion rejection.

**What this does NOT authorise.** Everything else in tier 2 stays gated. No PCB CAD, schematics, gerbers or case CAD; no RF antenna work, IPX, FCC/CE or drop testing; no ODM conversations; no silicon migration; no other tier-2 roadmap row. The § 71 cost discipline and the "don't build here" list in `apps/custom_watch/CLAUDE.md` bind unchanged — this entry moves exactly one row and names it.

**Precedence is a stated rule, not a race.** Two sensors can now report a pulse, so something has to decide. The rule: **a strap that is reporting a trusted rate no older than five seconds outranks the optical sensor; anything else falls back to the wrist; with neither, the watch blanks.** "Trusted" means the strap is not reporting *contact supported and not detected* (a strap on a table must never displace a wrist that is actually worn) and the rate sits inside the same 30–220 bpm physiological band the optical detector applies to its own estimate. Precedence is by sensor **class**, decided once: a chest strap measures the cardiac electrical signal directly, while wrist PPG is an optical proxy that is worst exactly where an ultra runner needs it — high-cadence descents, `vision.md` req #8 and the motion-artifact line of the bench checklist. The rejected alternative was a per-sample quality score, which neither source publishes: it would have to be invented, and an invented confidence figure flaps between sources mid-run.

**The seam that makes the rule enforceable.** Both producers used to be able to write `state::HR` and the last writer would win — precedence by scheduling accident. Each now publishes to its own watch (`HR_OPTICAL`, `HR_STRAP`) and a small `hr_source` arbiter task is the **single** publisher of `state::HR`. That costs one task and buys three things: the rule is evaluated in one place against `watch_core::hr_source::select_hr`, the optical task keeps reporting what the wrist sees even while the strap outranks it, and a strap still works when the optical sensor is absent entirely (the `hr` task parks on a failed I²C probe, which is exactly the bench case with nothing wired). The arbiter sleeps on its two inputs and arms exactly one timer — the deadline a held strap sample expires at — so a strap that simply stops still blanks on time with no polling and no free-running waker.

**The codec is pure and lives in `watch_core`.** `hr_source` holds the advertising-data filter, the Heart Rate Measurement (0x2A37) codec, the trust rules and the precedence rule; `app/src/tasks/hr_strap.rs` is radio glue with no decisions in it. This is the same split `ble_sync` was written under and for the same reason: the `ble` build gets no integration coverage at all, so every decision the transport makes has to be host-testable or it is untested. The 0x2A37 flags byte selects a uint8 or uint16 rate and declares two optional trailing fields, so the frame's length is a function of its own first byte — read the flags wrong and the *rate itself* comes out of the wrong offset. The decode is therefore strict in both directions: missing bytes are a truncated frame, leftover bytes mean the flags were not what the sender meant, and either rejects the frame whole. Advertising data gets the same treatment — a length byte that overruns the scan buffer ends the walk and reports "not a strap" rather than being indexed past or skipped over.

**Fail-closed, enumerated.** A malformed advertisement is not a strap. A malformed measurement publishes nothing and leaves the previous sample to age out on its own. A strap off the chest, or reporting 0 bpm as it settles, publishes no rate and the wrist takes over. A dropped link publishes an explicit `bpm: None` immediately rather than waiting out the staleness budget. And when *nothing* is authoritative the arbiter emits one synthesised blank — without it, a strap that drops on a watch with no optical sensor would leave its last rate on screen for a whole `hr_duty::hold_budget_s`, which is two minutes in Expedition, with nothing left to wake the consumer and correct it.

**Two SoftDevice-config consequences, one of them a real bench risk.** The watch is now a peripheral to the phone *and* a central to the strap, so `conn_count` goes 1 → 2 and one central role is declared. That raises the S140's RAM requirement above the peripheral-only figure. `memory-ble.x` reserves 31 KiB, a carried-over over-estimate from nrf-softdevice's six-connection example, and it is *expected* to still cover two connections at a 256-byte MTU — but only the device can say, because the SoftDevice reports the true RAM start at boot. **Confirming it is a bench item, not a claim.** Second: `central_sec_count` stays 0. Every strap on the market serves the Heart Rate Service unencrypted and the watch initiates no security as a central; a strap that demands encryption is out of scope at tier 1 and will fail to subscribe rather than silently downgrade. The strap link requests the 23-byte legacy-minimum ATT MTU, which is both all a measurement needs and what bounds the notification buffer — the GATT client's `heapless::Vec` panics rather than truncating if a notification arrives longer than its capacity, so the cap is derived from the MTU and pinned by a test.

**Deliberately not built.** Shutting the optical LED down while a strap is authoritative is the obvious power lever — LED drive dominates HR power — and it is not here. It changes the behaviour of the recording stack's HR layer on a path that has never run, and it needs a wake-latency design (a strap that drops leaves a ~15 s hole while the detector re-converges) that is not worth committing before any of this has been on a wrist. Also absent: strap-address persistence across a power cycle (each boot re-scans), running-dynamics or cycling-power sensors, and any UI for choosing between multiple straps in range — the first strap found offering the service wins.

**The verification ceiling, plainly.** The SoftDevice path **can never be sim-verified**: Renode cannot run proprietary Nordic firmware (§ 210), which is why BLE jumps host → build → bench with no rung in between, and `docs/custom_watch/quality_standards.md` says so for the whole step-6 block. So the GATT central role — the scan, the connect, the discovery, the subscription, every notification — is **build-verified only**. Nothing in it has executed. What *is* host-tested is the pure `hr_source` module: 38 tests over the advertising filter, the measurement codec, the trust rules, the precedence rule and the arbiter's publish decision, taking the suite 2154 → 2192 with no existing test changed. **Host-testing the codec proves the codec, not the radio.** The bench items this owes, on top of the existing step-6 list: that a real strap's advertisement passes the filter at all (some carry the service UUID only in the scan response, which arrives as a separate report), that the two-connection RAM figure fits the reservation, that a real measurement decodes, and that the precedence rule behaves when a strap is walked out of range mid-run with the optical sensor live.

## 366. A GGA may not complete a fix — and the register of GNSS/HR changes we refused for want of field data

**Date:** 2026-07-30

A hardening pass over the tier-1 GNSS and optical-HR paths, run under an explicit constraint: **there is no field-validation corpus** — zero real field hours — so a change was only allowed if it was justified by a specific failure case encoded as a test, and refused if it traded one failure mode for another without data to judge. Three changes shipped and a long list did not. **The refusals are the more valuable half of this entry**, because without them a future session re-derives each idea and re-does the same investigation to reach the same "cannot judge from here".

**The bug that was actually there.** `FixAccumulator::apply` emitted a completed fix on a **GGA** as well as an RMC. A u-blox receiver leads each 1 Hz epoch with GGA, so the accumulator re-published the *previous* epoch's position stamped with the *current* uptime, before that epoch's RMC arrived. Two consequences, both on the wrist: a runner at ~5 m/s read as zero displacement over a full second and so **alternated `Recording` / `Paused` every second** — against the step-7 bench item that asks for a steady `REC` — and because `Fix::uptime_s` is the only thing consumers age staleness against, a lone GGA after a gap republished a pre-gap position as current, which `elevation::rezero_reference`'s 5 s freshness gate then accepts. A GGA now enriches the next merge and returns `None`, which is what the module's own docs and `prop_fix.rs` already claimed it did. Strictly narrowing: no fix exists that did not before.

One existing test changed, and the change is the point: `other_sentences_are_ignored` probed "a GSV does not clear accumulated state" by asserting a *following GGA* emitted. That assertion was the defect being asserted as correct. It now probes the same subject with a following RMC.

Two smaller fail-closed guards: an NMEA numeric field past `f32` range read as `inf` (a checksum-valid field of ~39 digits — rare, but an infinite altitude wrote `i32::MAX` into the elevation profile *permanently*, since `thin()` keeps even indices and index 0 survives every thinning), and the recorder's GPS-altitude fallback in `feed_gap` now honours the `GPS_ALT_MIN_M`/`GPS_ALT_MAX_M` window the rest of the stack already applies — it was the one consumer trusting a number `elevation.rs` explicitly does not.

**Refused, with the reason, so nobody re-derives them:**

- **HDOP / GST accuracy-aware fix acceptance.** The parser already carries GSA's HDOP and GST's per-axis sigma and nothing consumes either. This is the real "my track drifted in the trees" lever — and every threshold is a tuning constant with no derivation. **This is the top field-data ask of the whole program.**
- **Bounding the § 330 re-anchor by `MAX_SPEED_MPS * dt`.** Today a `dt >= 10 s` re-anchor adopts *any* position, so a corrupt fix reaches the flash track. Bounding it makes a genuine >10 m/s transport gap (driving to the next aid station) take far longer to recover, and today's behaviour is better for that case. Undecidable without knowing how often a checksum-passing corrupt position occurs.
- **Ageing `current_speed_mps`.** It is the only GNSS-derived live value that never goes stale, so in a canyon with no fixes at all it holds forever, `is_moving()` stays true, and the barometric accumulator banks weather drift as vert — the exact phantom-vert failure its own doc claims to prevent. Not shipped because the gate also loses *genuine* baro vert for a runner climbing in a signal void, which is a core ultra scenario.
- **Optical HR: nothing shipped at all.** A refractory-spacing `div_ceil` fix was implemented, measured against a dicrotic-notch case at 25 and 100 Hz, found to make no observable difference *and* to convert a rejected super-physiological crossing into an accepted 214 bpm beat — a widening of acceptance — and reverted. Cadence-lock (an artifact at ~180 spm reads as a valid pulse) is unfixable without a second signal, and tier-1 hardware has no accelerometer. The `beat_ref` peak-hold blackout, the AGC rail-guard limit cycle, and the integer-EMA rounding asymmetry are all real and all need a PPG corpus or a PPK2 capture to judge.
- **`hr_duty`'s hold-vs-blank contract is a product call, not a data one.** The module says a held reading bridges one off-window, but the `hr` task publishes `None` the moment a freshly-reset detector is invalid, so the held value blanks at every window open — up to ~15 s of blank per minute in Balanced, earlier than the stated intent. The fix lives in the task, and the choice between an honest blank and bridging the convergence gap is the owner's.

**What this pass says about the verification ladder.** Every shipped change is host-tested and the GGA/RMC fix is additionally mutation-verified — the guard fails naming the defect when the `return None` is removed. None of it is bench-verified, and the refusal list is precisely the set of questions that only a wrist and a real receiver can close. § 82 is unchanged.

## 367. A signal void auto-pauses the recorder — the bug § 366 unmasked by fixing the one that hid it

**Date:** 2026-07-30

`Recorder` writes `state` in exactly one place: `on_fix`. Nothing ever paused on the **absence** of fixes, so a run that lost signal held `Recording` for as long as the void lasted — distance and moving time correctly frozen, the run view still telling the runner it was tracking them.

That had a guard, and the guard was passing. `ci_smoke.py`'s `dropout` scenario asserts every snapshot inside a 40 s void reads `paused`, and it went green on every run before this one. It was passing **vacuously**, for the reason [§ 366](#366-a-gga-may-not-complete-a-fix--and-the-register-of-gnsshr-changes-we-refused-for-want-of-field-data) removed: with a GGA completing a fix, each 1 Hz epoch led with a zero-displacement sample that failed `TRACK_THRESHOLD_M` and set `Paused`, and the RMC behind it arrived at the same `uptime_s`, hit the `dt == 0` duplicate gate, and returned before it could set anything. The recorder was pinned in `Paused` almost permanently. The void asserted `paused` and got it — from a recorder that was never in `Recording` to begin with.

So § 366's fix did not break the scenario. It removed the defect that was standing in for the missing feature, and the guard then reported the hole it was written to find. **A green guard over a broken mechanism is worth less than no guard**, because it also certifies everything downstream of it; this one had been signing off on lost-signal honesty since the day it was written.

The pause now happens in `tick`, which is the only thing that runs when nothing is arriving. The budget is `fix_interval_s * 3`, floored at 10 s, and is now shared with `route_position_stale` through one `fix_stale_budget_s` — the two must agree, or the view would claim to be tracking a runner whose course position it has already disowned. Gated on having had a fix at all, because `resume` also clears the anchor and pausing a just-resumed run before its first fix would fight the runner's own button.

**Moving the state is not the whole fix, and the first draft stopped there.** `rec_tag` renders a non-manual `Paused` by asking `is_moving()`, so with the state flipped and the speed untouched the tag still read a blinking `REC` for the entire void whenever the dropout began mid-stride — which is the realistic case and precisely the symptom being fixed. Speed cannot answer it: the last fix left the runner at 5 m/s and nothing since has been able to contradict that. So `Snapshot` now carries `signal_lost` beside `manual_paused`, which is the shape that field already established: the recorder knows *why* it paused and says so, instead of the face inferring it from a number that means something else. Both come off one `fix_stale()` predicate, so the state and its label cannot disagree.

**What it deliberately does not do.** It moves the state and the label, and nothing else. `is_moving` reads `current_speed_mps`, not the state, so the barometric vert accumulator is untouched — zeroing the speed here would have been precisely the "ageing `current_speed_mps`" change § 366 weighed and **refused**, and it would cost a runner their genuine vert while climbing through a canyon with no fixes, which is a core ultra case. The first draft of this change did zero it; the refusal register in § 366 is what caught it. A void is a statement about the GPS, not about whether the runner is still moving. A test pins that interaction so the auto-pause cannot quietly drift into the refused change.

Sim-verified: all 41 snapshots inside the void now read `paused`, and the § 330 re-anchor still resumes 3.0 s after it. Five host tests cover the boundary, the throttled-mode budget, the manual-pause interaction, the never-had-a-fix case, and the vert one above, plus a sixth over `rec_tag` for the tag itself. Both halves are mutation-verified: deleting the `tick` branch fails three of the recorder tests by name while the two negative cases correctly stay green, and deleting the `rec_tag` arm fails the tag test with `REC` where `AUTO` belongs.

The tag half is the part a passing test suite would not have caught on its own — the recorder tests assert `RecordState` and `is_moving()`, and every one of them stays green while the wrist still reads `REC`. It took reading the render layer to find it. Worth remembering that "the state machine is correct" and "the runner is told the truth" are two claims, and only the second one is the requirement.

## 368. Demo data that never reaches the surface it demos is not demo data — the §359 crest rail, and the observability it needed

**Date:** 2026-07-30

Three sim scenarios had run the climb pages for weeks without asserting a single thing about them, and closing that turned up two reasons why, both worth recording.

**The subsystem had no observable.** `climb.rs` is reached only through `Snapshot::climb`, and the app logged nothing about it. The sim's whole assertion surface is decoded defmt output, so the only claim available was a page dump — and by [§ 314](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md)'s own rule a non-blank frame is not a correct number. The detector's output and the crest read were therefore unassertable outside host tests, and `terrain`'s existing "the Climb page is in the cycle" proved less than it looks: that page opens on a live ascent **or** a crest ahead, so it cannot separate the two halves, and a data-presence bit wired to the wrong field passes it. Two `debug!` lines fixed that. They cost nothing on the wrist — `.cargo/config.toml` pins `DEFMT_LOG = "info"`, so a `debug!` is compiled out of the hardware build; the sim asks for `debug` explicitly.

**Gate each half on its own change.** The first version logged both halves whenever the `ClimbView` as a whole changed. The active half is baro-fed and moves constantly, so an unchanged crest was re-emitted alongside it — which downstream reads as *a crest that stopped closing*, the exact symptom a stale along-course position produces. The scenario caught it immediately, which is the argument for asserting a trend rather than a value: the assertion found a defect in the observability added to serve it, before either reached a wrist.

**And the demo data pointed the wrong way.** `SIM_COURSE_ELEV_M` put the summit at the course's middle point. Both NMEA fixtures start at that middle point and run the east leg away from it, so the only crest on the course was one the runner had already crossed and `crest_ahead` correctly returned `None` for the entire run — the rail could not be armed in the sim at all, no matter what asserted it. The summit moved to the last point. This is the same fix as the GSA fix-type transitions added to `gps_dropout.nmea` in the 2026-07-19 pass, which the honest signal meter needed before it was testable, and the same lesson: **sim demo data is only demo data if it actually reaches the surface it is demonstrating**, and "the page renders" is not evidence that it does.

The crest is asserted as a falling series — distance and metres-still-to-climb both monotonically decreasing across the approach — rather than as a value. `record.rs`'s own doc comment explains why: a position frozen by a lost signal keeps reporting the crest from where the runner was, so the one number on the page they would act on stops falling while they climb. A single sample cannot tell that from a live read. Mutation-verified by freezing the along-course position: the run yields one reading instead of thirty-two and the guard names the position as the cause.
## 369. Recovery time is derived on the watch from a number it was already being pushed — and the layoff gate travels as a verdict, not as history

**Date:** 2026-07-30

The roadmap row "Training status / readiness / recovery time" had two of its three parts. `fitness::days_until_next_hard_session` — the port of web's `daysUntilNextHardSession`, which projects ATL/CTL forward with no added stress and returns the easy days still owed — had been ported and host-tested since 2026-07-11 and was called by nothing. The Fitness page showed the recovery *verdict* (`REST` / `EASY` / `SWEET`) with no forward half, which is the half a runner actually plans around: "what is today for" is a smaller question than "how long am I still paying for yesterday".

Nothing new had to reach the watch for it. The rolling CTL/ATL/TSB trio has arrived through `Recorder::set_load_trend` since § 352, and ATL + CTL are exactly the projection's two inputs — so the line is derived at render time from data already on the device, with no new `SET1` field, no new setter, and no growth in the push. That is worth naming because the reflex on this workspace's history-derived pages has been to add a pushed view; here the pushed view already existed one page over.

**The layoff gate is the non-obvious part.** Web withholds the countdown for a runner returning from a break — their ATL decayed faster than their CTL, so the trend reads fresh when it is really detrained, and a date on which they are "cleared to go hard" is the worst possible thing to hand them. Web decides this with `isReturningFromLayoff(runs)` over run history the watch does not hold and will not hold at tier 1. But web feeds that same boolean into `recoveryAdvice`, so the phone's answer is already on the wrist as `RecoveryAdvice::ReturningFromLayoff` in the pushed `FitnessView`. The watch reads the *verdict* where web reads the *history* — the same question, answered once, upstream. A test pins that the suppression is the verdict and not the numbers: the identical trend projects three days without it.

The other two withholdings are web's verbatim: no rolling load synced (nothing to project), and an answer of zero (already recovered — the verdict beside the label has said so, and `~0 DAYS` reads as a countdown that never started).

**No new glance page, deliberately.** Web puts this line on the same Fitness card as the recovery verdict, and the watch's Fitness page is that card's mirror with three free rows. A 38th page would charge the § 350 press-cost — one more stop in the BTN3/BTN4 cycle, on every lap of it — to separate a number from the verdict it qualifies. [§ 24](#24-web-is-the-canonical-feature-surface-mobile-and-watches-are-platform-additive) also settles what is *not* built: Garmin's third metric in this trio, **Training Status** (Productive / Peaking / Overreaching / Unproductive), has no web equivalent, so the watch does not get to invent one — that row stays a web-first item, not a firmware gap.

Host-tested: four face tests over the three-day and one-day projections, the already-recovered suppression, and the layoff suppression, plus a fifth assertion on the existing no-load-synced case. Nothing above host — the projection reaches a panel only in a fixture, and no scenario arms the Fitness page (it has no `SET1` field), so this claims nothing about the wrist.
## 370. A generated loop reaches the wrist through route detail's export menu, not the builder's Generate button

**Date:** 2026-07-30

The watch has rendered a pushed course since [§ 335](#335-the-crs1-course-frame-gets-a-mandatory-crc32-and-unlike-set1-its-pre-crc-versions-stop-decoding) sealed `CRS1` v3 — Nav page, off-course alert, turn cues, climb profile, crest-ahead. The phone has generated loops for longer still (the mobile builder's OSRM bisection; the `graph_cycle` sidecar behind web's `/api/routes/generate`). Neither end was missing. What was missing was any way for a runner to join them: the only `pushCourse` call site in the app was the canned three-point demo on the dev Sim Watch screen, which pushes the same Boulder rectangle no matter what the runner has saved.

**The affordance belongs to the route, not to the generate.** The obvious place is a "send to watch" button next to Generate in the route builder, and it is the wrong one: it would work for ten seconds after a generate and never again. A loop generated yesterday, a GPX a friend shared, a route a club published, a run saved as a route — all still stranded, and the row would read closed. So it goes in route detail's share menu, beside Share link / image / GPX / GPX+markers / KML. A course is another export target for a route; that menu is where the export targets already live, and the star-for-watch toggle is two icons away in the same AppBar. The generated loop reaches it the way every other route does — Save, then open it.

**It reads the clipped polyline, not the row.** `_displayWaypoints` is `widget.route.waypoints` for an owner and `clip_route_for_viewer`'s output for everyone else ([§ 33](#33-privacy-zones-live-in-user_settings-clipping-is-client-side-nearby-leak-is-a-known-v1-gap)). The push reads that, for the same reason the GPX exporter does: a non-owner sending a public route to their own wrist would otherwise carry the owner's unclipped trace out over the radio. The radio is just another way out of the app, and the invariant does not care which one.

**The budget is met by priority Douglas–Peucker, not by decimation and not by a cut.** `capCoursePoints` already existed as an even-index sampler and its own doc said a route with real geometry should prefer an RDP simplifier first; that simplifier did not exist. `simplifyToBudget` is DP run by priority rather than by tolerance — keep both endpoints, then restore whichever dropped point sits furthest from the chord that replaced it, until the 256-point budget is spent. Even decimation fits too, but it spends the budget uniformly, as much of it on a straight as on a switchback, and the switchbacks are the geometry a breadcrumb exists to show. It is deliberately **not** part of the `route_simplify.ts` ↔ `route_simplify.dart` parity pair, on the same footing as `computeElevationLoss`: web has no fixed-capacity course consumer, so there is nothing to mirror.

**Both failure directions are doors, not silences.** A route the frame cannot hold is thinned and the runner is told from how many points to how many; a route with fewer than two positions is refused with a sentence. Nothing truncates. A course that stops at position 256 of 4,000 hands the watch a breadcrumb ending in the middle of nowhere *and* an off-course alert calibrated against it — strictly worse than the honest `NO COURSE LOADED` the watch shows with no course at all, because the watch has no way to notice it was shortchanged. The elevation series is all-or-nothing for the same reason: the firmware wants one sample per point, and filling a gap would draw a climb the route does not have, so one missing sample drops the whole profile and the climb pages stay honestly empty.

**Gated on the loopback backend, like the Sim Watch link ([§ 209](#209-the-watch-sim-runs-the-whole-tier-1-experience-emulated-display-sim-phone-link-dev-gated-mobile-screen)).** The custom watch is research-tier with no unit in anyone's hands ([§ 71](#71-own-hardware-an-ultra-marathon-watch-stays-research-only-watch-development-is-deferred-indefinitely)), so a "Send to watch" row in every user's share menu would advertise hardware that does not exist and fail for all of them. The whole code path is built and tested; the gate lives in config and defaults closed. It lifts when there is a watch to send to.

**What this is verified to:** *host-tested* only, per [`quality_standards.md`](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md). 10 tests pin the budget simplifier, 7 the route→course shaping, 7 the screen (both sides of the gate, the unchanged push, the thinned push, the refusal, a failed write, and the non-owner clip). The bytes that leave the phone are the same `encodeCourse` output the frozen `CRS1` goldens pin against the firmware's own. **None of it is bench-verified and none of it can be** — no BLE stack runs in the sim ([§ 210](#210-tier-1-ble-s140-softdevice-is-a-compile-verified-feature-gated-build--mutually-exclusive-with-the-sim-off-by-default)) and no hardware exists. That a real watch loads a real generated loop is a bench item, on the same list as every other radio claim.

## 371. A guard for something that would also happen on its own has to be timed on the emulator's clock — the workout scenario, and the alert slot it had to clear first

**Date:** 2026-07-30

The § 354 structured-workout runner had been carrying a *sim-verified* rung since the day it landed, earned by walking the sim's demo workout by hand under `bench_jog`. That was real evidence and it was worth nothing two days later, because nothing re-ran it. A hand session certifies the afternoon it happened; only a scenario certifies the branch. `ci_smoke.py` grows a `workout` scenario, which was the last major run-view rail without one.

Most of it is the shape the file already had — wait on a task's own defmt line, walk the cycle, dump a panel, assert the flush. Two of its claims are not, and both are worth recording because the reasoning generalises to any scenario over an interval-driven subsystem.

**The lap press's observable is the observable it would get for free.** §354 makes BTN5's tap double as *skip the active step*, and the way you see a skip is a `record: alert WorkoutStep` line. But the auto-advance produces exactly that same line when the step ends by itself. So the obvious assertion — press BTN5, then wait for a transition — passes against a firmware whose press does nothing at all: wait long enough and the step ends regardless. That is a guard that cannot fail, which is worse than no guard, because it also signs off on everything downstream of it (the § 367 lesson, one scenario earlier).

What separates the two is **when**. On this fixture the steps the press displaces are 50 m and 60 m, and credited distance accrues at ~1.5 m/s — about half of each ~2.97 m hop is absorbed by the 3.0 m `TRACK_THRESHOLD_M` — so they need ~33 s and ~40 s to settle on their own. The press's edge is asserted inside 15 s of the step's start, measured against the transition line that opened it. Observed at **0.6 s and 0.4 s**; with `Recorder::lap`'s `skip_step` call deleted the same edge arrives at **30.4 s** and the assertion names the auto-advance as the cause.

**And the clock has to be the firmware's, not the harness's.** Renode's virtual clock runs at a ratio to wall time that swings with host load — § 362 measured it between ~1x and ~2x on one machine in one afternoon — so a wall-clock bound says nothing about how much of a step was left to run. The gap is read off the decoded stream's own virtual timestamps, the same discipline `dropout` adopted for its void after a wall-clock window was tried and rejected there.

One consequence is counter-intuitive enough to state: the *wait* for that edge is deliberately **longer** than the step it displaces (90 s against ~33 s). A shorter wait is not safer — it just means a broken firmware fails on a bare "no line matched" timeout, which says something did not arrive and nothing about what. Waiting past the step puts the auto-advance's own edge in hand so the timing assertion can do the diagnosis. Both were run; the first version of this scenario used a 30 s wait and produced exactly the uninformative red.

**A count is only a claim about a gate while nothing else can take the slot.** The end-of-step warning is gated — `ENDING_MIN_STEP_M` is 100 m, so the demo plan's four 50-60 m distance steps cannot earn one, and `ENDING_MIN_STEP_S` is 20 s, so its 30 s recovery alone can. That makes "exactly one warning across the plan" a claim about the gate itself, where "at least one fired" would pass a runner that warned on every step. But the alert slot is single and shared: with the sim's shortened fuel / distance / time / pace arms in it, a count of anything is a count of traffic. So the scenario boots `--no-alerts` — the § 362 feature split, reused for a purpose it was not built for — and what remains in the slot is exactly and only the workout rail. The same flag keeps a fuel banner off the two Workout page dumps, since a banner owns the hero band. Arbitration *between* a workout banner and a fuel one stays `alerts`' surface; this scenario deliberately declines to have an opinion about it.

This half was falsified too, by dropping `ENDING_MIN_STEP_M` from 100 m to 10 m: the scenario reports **three** warnings where one belongs, and the log shows exactly the defect the gate's own doc comment names — a 50 m step is already inside the 50 m warning window at the instant it starts, so the runner is told a step is ending 0.9 s after it began.

**What it does not earn.** Nothing here reads a glyph, so `NOT SYNCED` and `WORKOUT DONE` stay host-test claims about `face.rs` — the page's presence in the cycle is `Snapshot::pages_mask`'s `workout.is_some()` bit and its render is ink, not text. The `WKT1` radio leg can never be sim-verified (§ 210 / § 314): the scenario arms over the channel the ble task publishes on, not over the characteristic. And it cannot assert the negative — "the Workout page stays OUT of a cycle with no workout" — because every run-starting boot in the harness arms the demo workout, so there is no session in which to make that claim. The § 82 Definition of Done is untouched; the rail stays unticked in the parity backlog until the bench.

No firmware behaviour moved. The scenario reads defmt lines that already existed, and the two production files the falsification runs disturbed (`record.rs`, `workout.rs`) were reverted before the batch landed.

## 372. Backyard-ultra mode: the bell is the clock's, the loop is the lap's, and the corral is the race director's

**Date:** 2026-07-30

The last-person-standing format sends one fixed loop off every hour **on the hour** and scores on **loop count**. A runner must complete the loop and be back in the corral before the next bell; whistles sound at 3, 2 and 1 minutes to it; the event runs until one runner remains. Nothing a Garmin or a COROS ships models any of it, which is why [`roadmap.md § New wedges`](../custom_watch/roadmap.md#new-wedges--nobody-ships-these) tracks it as a differentiator rather than parity. `watch_core::backyard` plus a Backyard glance page builds the wrist half. Four decisions are worth recording, and one refusal matters more than any of them.

**The bell is anchored to the wall clock, never to elapsed time.** The countdown is `3600 - (local_time_of_day % 3600)`, derived from the receiver's UTC clock shifted by the phone-pushed timezone offset and extrapolated on uptime between fixes — the same shaping [`daylight`](../custom_watch/navigation.md) already uses. The tempting alternative is to anchor on the run's start or on the last lap: both are wrong in the same way, and wrong *cumulatively*. A runner who crawls in at 59:30 and leaves 30 s late has a 59:30 loop, not a fresh hour; anchoring on their departure would hand them a countdown that drifts a little every loop and is minutes off by loop 20 — which in this format is the difference between a rest and an elimination. The modulus form also needs no date, so it survives midnight, and a backyard runs for days.

**Requiring the pushed timezone is the honesty cost, and it is worth paying.** UTC and local hour boundaries coincide almost everywhere, and "almost" is exactly the word this firmware refuses. In a +05:30 zone a UTC-anchored countdown is thirty minutes wrong — a runner told they have forty minutes when they have ten. So the page refuses in the two cases the shaping can fail, separately and by name: no timezone reads `NOT SYNCED`, no receiver clock reads `AWAITING FIX`, and the hero reads `--:--`. Same split, same words, same reason as the Daylight countdown.

**The loop rides the recorder's lap; it is not a second counter.** A loop boundary IS a lap close — the same `close_lap` that banks a split to flash and syncs to the phone — and while the mode is armed the **bell drives the auto-lap in place of the runner's chosen trigger**. A classic 6.706 km loop crosses six kilometre lines, so leaving the distance auto-lap on would bury the loop splits the phone reads as the runner's result under thirty-six identical fragments.

**That suppression is total, across every rung § 374 added** — this paragraph was written against the hard-coded `AUTO_LAP_DISTANCE_M` that § 374 replaced in the same integration, so it owes an answer for the seven rungs it never saw. The answer is the same for all of them: an armed bell returns from `check_auto_lap` before either axis is read. A 5-minute rung is in fact the *worse* case the kilometre made — twelve empty closes per hour-long loop against a 64-record store, evicting the loop splits that ARE the result, which is exactly § 374's own "empty laps displace real ones" argument one notch sharper. `Off` needs no special case: it already closes nothing, so an armed bell over it leaves precisely the bell and the button. The runner's choice is **dormant, not cleared** — it lives in `CFG1` and in the `SET1` v7 field, and disarming the mode restores it mid-run — so arming a backyard never costs a runner the trigger they set for the rest of their season. Two tests pin it: a time rung suppressed then restored on disarm, and an `Off` rung whose BTN5 press still closes a loop. The runner's BTN5 press keeps its one meaning (close a lap) and is *read* as the corral return, which stands that window's bell lap down; BTN5 grew no third tier and the §350 grammar is untouched. Two consequences fall out and both are deliberate: at most one loop is counted per bell window, so a fat-fingered second press at hour 30 cannot inflate the scored number; and the count is therefore "bells this run closed a loop on", which for a runner still in the race is their loop count.

**The loop's length is learned, not configured.** A five-button watch is a poor place to enter 6706 metres, and events differ. The runner runs loop 1; from loop 2 the mean of the loops closed so far *is* the loop, and the projected return margin comes off it plus the live pace. Loop 1 has no margin and says `--` rather than guessing, as does a runner with no live pace — the [`cutoff_eta`](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md) rule that a stale input withholds the number instead of dressing it up. In the corral the margin is absent entirely rather than zero: `0:00` there would read as "you only just made it" when the honest statement is that there is nothing left to project.

**The refusal: the watch never declares a runner in or out.** It would be easy — the bell passed, no return was marked, so call it. It would also be a lie in the one place a lie is unforgivable. The corral is the race director's, the timing mat is theirs, and a runner who crossed the line at 59:58 without reaching for a button has not been eliminated by their watch's opinion. So there is no `DNF` verdict, no elimination banner, and no "you will not make it" claim anywhere in the mode — only the margin, the countdown, and the count, each withheld when its inputs are missing. The app's own `is_dnf` modelling stays where it belongs: with whoever ran the race.

**Arming lives on the watch, in the settings menu, idle-only.** No `SET1` field and no version bump: a backyard runner arms this at a start line in a field, and the menu is exactly the §351 surface for a setting a runner changes without a phone. It persists in a spare `CFG1` flag bit with no companion "set" bit — disarmed is the default, so a clear bit already says what an unset choice would, and every pre-§372 record decodes as a watch that is not in a backyard. Idle-only is not a limitation but the point: arming re-points the auto-lap, so a run has to be wholly inside the mode or wholly outside it. The sixth row cost the §351 press bound nothing, because it went in at the ring's far seat — a 6-ring's cursor distances are `[0,1,2,3,2,1]` against the 5-ring's `[0,1,2,2,1]`, so **every pre-existing row keeps its exact cost** and the new 5-press maximum belongs to the one row touched once per race. Six rows also fill the panel exactly, so a seventh needs a layout rather than a push, and a test pins that.

**The whistles ride the existing alert slot.** `Alert::BackyardBell(min)` goes through the same `AlertEngine` as everything else — one banner at a time, TTL 8 s — as a **drop-not-queue** arm, the milestone rule: a `3 MIN` banner read at 1:40 is a lie about the clock, and the page carries the live countdown anyway. It sits one rung under the zone ceiling and above pace, fuel and milestones, because missing the bell ends the race outright with nothing left to correct afterwards. It is deliberately *not* gated on `Recording`: the runner the whistle is most for is the one auto-paused in the corral with sixty seconds left.

**Rung.** Host-tested (24 tests over the core, plus recorder, face, alert and menu coverage) and build-verified for `thumbv7em-none-eabihf` across the default, `ble` and sim feature sets. **Not sim-verified, and cannot be today**: every NMEA fixture carries a few minutes of clock, so no Renode scenario can reach a bell at all — the first thing owed is a fixture that can. The bench checklist item in [`quality_standards.md`](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md) names what only hardware settles, including the uptime-extrapolation drift between fixes, which is an open value.

## 373. Sleep-station mode computes the nap from the race, refuses to guess at it, and does not claim to wake anyone
